The Paradox of Dollar Dominance

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2955 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • ESWAR PRASAD is a Professor at Cornell University, a Senior Fellow at the Brookings Institution, and the author of The Doom Loop: Why the World Economic Order Is Spiraling Into Disorder.
  • TONY ZHANG is an Associate Professor at Arizona State University.
  • This article is based on a paper the authors prepared for the August 2026 Jackson Hole Economic Policy Symposium.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

GORDON LIAO is Chief Economist at Circle.

ESWAR PRASAD is a Professor at Cornell University, a Senior Fellow at the Brookings Institution, and the author of The Doom Loop: Why the World Economic Order Is Spiraling Into Disorder.

TONY ZHANG is an Associate Professor at Arizona State University.

This article is based on a paper the authors prepared for the August 2026 Jackson Hole Economic Policy Symposium.

How Technology Is—and Isn’t—Changing the Global Economy.

Gordon Liao, Eswar Prasad, and Tony Zhang.

It is no secret that much of the world is eager to escape from the clutches of the dollar-dominated global financial system. For over a century, that system has given the United States enormous financial clout, which it has wielded in applying financial sanctions against its adversaries and, in recent decades, to borrow money to fund its budget and trade deficits. For decades, foreign governments have tried to weaken the dollar’s grip, but they have had little success in establishing their currencies as a legitimate alternative.

Now, a new force has emerged that could shake things up: technology. Financial innovations, especially in digital currencies and electronic payment systems, could finally give other currencies a better chance of competing with the dollar. These innovations are making it easier and cheaper to exchange currencies directly for one another rather than using the dollar as an intermediary currency.

But for all the new opportunities these innovations create for currency exchange, reduced frictions in global transactions might only reinforce the dollar’s dominance. Even if costs decrease for using dollar alternatives, foreign investors will not capitalize on them if those countries’ financial markets remain unsteady and their institutions weak. As U.S. government debt soars, the country’s rule of law erodes, and the Federal Reserve’s independence comes into question, the dollar’s dominance may seem uncertain. But the dollar could remain supreme by default.

Continued dollar dominance could lead to further global economic turmoil, as the United States antagonizes its trading partners and persists with undisciplined policies that result in large budget deficits and trade deficits. There is a chance that the dollar, too, loses the trust of foreign investors—a prospect of comeuppance that would no doubt be received with glee in many capitals. But governments should be careful what they wish for. A world bereft of a reliable currency of last resort at times of global financial panic could be even more unstable than one dominated by Washington.

According to recent reports, the U.S. dollar should be losing its dominance in global finance for a host of reasons. First is the country’s penchant for weaponizing its currency. Across administrations, Washington has imposed financial sanctions on rivals, such as Iran and Russia, cutting off their access to dollar transactions and thereby kneecapping their foreign trade. The economies of U.S. allies sometimes get tangled up in these sanctions, too, when the U.S. government threatens to use secondary sanctions to cut off their banks and corporations from access to dollars in order to deter third parties from transacting with the sanctioned countries. In 2014, for instance, U.S. authorities penalized the French bank BNP Paribas for processing dollar payments on behalf of clients in Cuba, Iran, and Sudan. The French government protested the fine to no avail. In light of such heavy-handed behavior, government officials and central bankers outside the United States have hardly been shy about their intentions to reduce their dollar dependence.

According to recent reports, washington’s broader policy choices, especially the lack of fiscal discipline, should also be undermining confidence in American financial markets. U.S. federal government debt now exceeds $40 trillion, nearly 125 percent of the country’s annual GDP, and there are scant signs that Washington is trying to rein it in. Such high debt levels usually lead to some combination of high inflation, soaring interest expenditures, and currency depreciation. The Trump administration’s hostile approach to international trade, including with close allies, is also causing governments to consider “de-risking” their economic ties to the United States. President Donald Trump’s open attacks on the independence of the Federal Reserve and weakening of checks and balances are eroding the pillars of the U.S. institutional system that underlies foreign investors’ trust in the dollar.

It has been revealed that and indeed, there are some signs of the dollar’s decline. The currency’s share of foreign exchange reserves held by foreign central banks has fallen from 71 percent in 2000 to 57 percent today. Yields on U.S. Treasury securities—the asset long seen as the ultimate safe haven for investors during financial turmoil—have risen, meaning investors are demanding a higher return for lending to the U.S. government. In October, the yield on ten-year Treasury notes hit 5.3 percent, the highest level since 2002.

Recent findings suggest that in most other dimensions, however, the dollar looks as dominant as ever. Sixty percent of cross-border transactions are denominated in dollars when excluding the eurozone, which is defined by the common use of the euro, and that number has only gone up in recent years. The euro’s share of cross-border payments outside the eurozone now stands at about 13 percent, and the renminbi’s is less than three percent. The dollar remains preeminent in most other measures of a currency’s international usage, too, including its share of trading activity in foreign exchange markets and denomination of international debt securities, which corporations use to raise funds in global capital markets.

It has been revealed that in short, no serious rivals to the dollar have emerged. The reason is simple: other major currencies look even shakier than the dollar. Traditional reserve currencies such as the euro, the yen, and the pound sterling have been undermined by their countries’ weak economies and political instability. Although currencies such as the Australian and Canadian dollars, the Swedish krona, and the Swiss franc have filled in some of the gap, each of these is too small to be consequential in global finance. The dollar’s most discussed putative rival, the renminbi, has also faded. Beijing has done little to alleviate the Chinese economy’s deep-rooted problems, including a prolonged property market slump, high levels of local government debt, and tight government control over the economy and financial markets. Moreover, the Chinese government has been unwilling to allow for the free flow of money across its borders or for market forces to determine its currency’s exchange rate. The renminbi has, in turn, failed to garner greater international use. The result is a second tier of currencies that is increasingly fragmented, with none able to pose any real challenge to the reigning currency hegemon.

In the era of modern financial markets, one of the main purposes of an international currency has been to facilitate indirect transactions among different currencies. It has long been easier and cheaper for a Chinese importer of Brazilian iron ore to exchange renminbi for dollars and pay for the ore in dollars and for the Brazilian exporter to then convert those dollars into Brazilian reais. This is because cross-border payments have long been dominated by a dollar-based global banking network, making dollars the most plentiful currency to conduct payments with. But in recent years, digital technologies have created cheaper and quicker pathways for moving money across borders.

In a recent development, one critical innovation has been the tokenization of money and financial assets, which has been facilitated by technology called blockchain. Blockchain, essentially a public digital ledger that is managed by a computer algorithm rather than by a single bank or clearinghouse, offers a platform for tokenized assets to trade. It does not matter which country the parties are located in, as long as they have Internet access. In the last few years, tokenization has expanded to include not just cash but also financial assets such as government bonds, equities, and mutual funds.

In a recent development, in theory, these changes have the potential to reshuffle the international currency order. Over the past few years, countries such as Brazil, China, India, and Russia have been conducting more trade in their own currencies by building their own cross-border payment networks and linking them to one another, in an effort to reduce their reliance on the dollar. The quantity of these transactions is still modest, because the currencies have limited use outside their countries, and it is still easier and cheaper to transact in a well-recognized and widely accepted currency such as the dollar. But as the countries’ payment systems and financial markets develop further, that number could increase dramatically, altering the currency landscape. Blockchain-based financial innovations could add momentum.

Cross-border investment could become much easier, too. Presently, investing in foreign securities involves going through brokers and other middlemen who demand hefty fees and take days to process transactions. But the tokenization of bonds and equities has expanded investors’ access to a broader swath of international financial assets, even in emerging-market and developing economies, where financial markets tend to be small, thinly traded, and not well connected to global trading networks. In the same way, it has expanded the access of entrepreneurs and small businesses to global pools of capital previously out of their reach, which could particularly help businesses in countries with underdeveloped financial markets. Bank deposits are likely to be available in tokenized form soon, too, which will make it easier to conduct transactions through more traditional payment channels.

But the spread of tokenization might strengthen the dollar’s dominance rather than weaken it. The example of stablecoins illustrates this paradox. Whereas cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin are created and distributed by a computer algorithm, meaning they have nothing anchoring their value, the value of a stablecoin is typically pegged to an official currency. This value is stable because it is backed one to one by stores of safe and liquid assets—usually government bonds, bank deposits, and cash. Those assets are usually denominated in the dollar. More than $250 billion in stablecoins is now in circulation, and over 99 percent of that value is tied to the dollar. As long as the dollar remains preeminent, investors will have little incentive to back stablecoins with any other currency.

Recent findings suggest that dollar-denominated stablecoins are a boon for the United States. By solidifying the dollar’s central position in international payments, rising demand for dollar-backed stablecoins also indirectly fuels demand for Treasury securities, lowering the yields the U.S. government has to offer investors to buy those securities and making it easier to fund U.S. budget deficits. Other payment innovations could make it even cheaper to use the dollar for cross-border transactions, minimizing the relative advantage that such innovations provide other currencies. Financial innovations built on new technologies cannot by themselves make up for other currencies’ existing weaknesses—namely, the weak economies and institutions that back them up.

Industry observers note that there is another major shift underway in the global economy that favors the dollar’s fortunes and that financial innovations are likely only to reinforce. In the first two decades of this century, central banks—particularly those of large emerging-market economies such as China and India—acquired vast troves of foreign assets denominated in hard currencies such as the euro, pound sterling, Japanese yen, and, most of all, the dollar to increase their foreign exchange reserves. These reserves helped those central banks cope with volatility in capital flows and exchange rates, which is a recurring hazard for countries that fall in and out of favor with foreign investors—often because of factors beyond their control, such as changes in U.S. interest rates. But in the last few years, central banks have stopped adding to their reserve stockpiles or have begun diversifying into other assets, such as gold, because they are reluctant to increase their investments in a country with fickle economic and geopolitical policies. In 2010, foreign central banks accounted for 70 percent of U.S. Treasuries held by foreign investors, a share that has dropped to about 40 percent as demand has leveled off. The retreat of these once reliable sources of demand threatens Washington’s ability to borrow cheaply.

Luckily for the United States, there is an alternative force that is more than making up for this loss in demand. As the costs to cross-border asset trade fall because of financial innovations, private investors from both advanced and emerging-market countries are increasing their foreign investments in search of higher returns and to diversify their portfolios. And they are flocking to dollar assets, from Treasuries to corporate bonds to equities, because U.S. financial markets offer an unmatched combination of good returns, low trading costs, and legal protections. In the present decade, net inflows of financial capital into the United States have been positive for practically every quarter. Despite chatter about de-risking and diversification since Trump’s election, these inflows have only ramped up in recent years.

Greater financial innovation will intensify rather than reverse these trends, delivering yet another blow to countries seeking to strengthen their currencies and counter dollar weaponization. These trends may hurt small and institutionally weak countries most of all. Those around the world who have long trusted the dollar more than their own currencies now have easier access to it—and they are likely to use it. Increased use of dollar-backed payment systems and investments in dollar assets could cause those countries to cede their monetary sovereignty, weakening their central banks’ ability to steer domestic interest rates and inflation. This phenomenon of “dollarization” has long been rampant in parts of Latin America, which have suffered repeated bouts of high inflation and which, through trade, tourism, and remittances from emigrants, have ready access to dollar cash. Financial innovation could also spread that phenomenon to other corners of the developing world, concentrating even more of the world’s savings—and its financial risks—in a single currency managed by a single central bank.

It has been revealed that in theory, the best, most stable international monetary system would be truly multipolar, with no single currency in a position of dominance but with several major currencies—each backed by deep financial markets, sound economic policies, and trustworthy institutions—anchoring international trade and finance. In the period before World War I, the British pound sterling, the French franc, and the German mark all denominated transactions and served as reserve currencies. When trouble struck, although sporadically, the countries’ central banks supported one another, helping to stave off broader financial panic. Renewed currency competition would force the competing governments, including the United States, to adopt responsible policies to avoid their currencies being shunned by investors. But given the economic and institutional malaise plaguing China, Japan, the United Kingdom, and the eurozone, such an outcome seems unlikely.

Industry observers note that if the dollar loses its position of privilege and no single currency is able to replace it, the global currency system will become even more fragmented than it is now. Such a scenario could unfold if U.S. debt grew so large that investors began doubting its value and dumped it, if additional sanctions and tariffs drove countries to shun the dollar despite the costs, or if the Fed’s independence were seriously compromised, leading to a surge in inflation and a plunge in the dollar’s value. As things stand, if the dollar lost its position of privilege, it would be replaced not by a handful of strong currencies but by a number of weak ones, none backed by sufficiently robust financial markets or a central bank able and willing to serve as the world’s lender of last resort during a crisis.

It has been revealed that if the global economic system has no currency to anchor global investors’ trust, stress in financial markets could spiral into unstoppable turmoil. During the global financial crisis of 2008–9, for example, the Fed pumped a huge number of dollars into U.S. and international financial markets to prop up banks and corporations around the world that desperately needed dollars to meet their debt obligations and reinforce their balance sheets. Even though the United States had been the epicenter of the crisis, trust in the Fed helped prevent a terrible situation from becoming even worse. Investors who were anxious about the safety of their assets piled into Treasuries, an investment they trusted would be returned.

Greater dollar dominance, then, is the most likely scenario for the future. The danger of this outcome is that the United States will have even less incentive than before to be more fiscally responsible. If foreign investors remain eager to invest in U.S. financial markets, Washington will have little reason to reduce its budget and trade deficits. Fed policies, including interest rate changes, could cause whiplash effects for other countries. In 2013, for example, the mere prospect of the Fed reducing measures to keep U.S. interest rates low sent currencies in Brazil, India, Indonesia, and Turkey tumbling because investors around the world began anticipating higher returns on U.S. assets and pulled their money out of those countries’ stocks and bonds. As capital flows in and out of markets in response to the Fed’s actions rather than in response to their own monetary policy, other countries could be left bereft of policy tools to stabilize their economies and financial markets in such a scenario. Emerging-market and developing economies, which have shallow financial markets and rely heavily on foreign borrowing, often in dollars, are especially vulnerable to volatile capital flows and exchange rates. In a world of greater dollar dominance, those countries could face more frequent currency crises, capital flight, and debt distress.

As disconcerting as the dollar’s continued preeminence might seem, however, the world needs a currency it can trust. As threats to international financial stability accelerate, financial markets can ill afford to be left adrift. One way or another, the world will have to learn to live with currency disorder, and the dollar, at least for now, is the least bad option.

Industry observers note that the Iran war appears to be heating up (again), as diplomatic talks have hit a wall (again). The United States and Iran resumed strikes over the past week, ending a roughly two-month lull in the conflict.

The renewed fighting has come as Iran continues to attack shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and amid an ongoing U.S. blockade on Iranian oil exports.

Tit-for-tat. Over the past six days, Iran launched a series of strikes on U.S. assets in Bahrain, which hosts the U.S. Navy’s 5th Fleet, and an air base in Kuwait that hosts U.S. forces.

In a recent development, iran targeted a U.S. early warning radar facility in Bahrain on Friday and took aim at a radar system at a helicopter base in the tiny island nation on Sunday. No damage was reported. Tehran noted the attacks were in retaliation for U.S. strikes on Iranian communications towers as well as ongoing drone surveillance operations.

It has been revealed that on Tuesday, Iran targeted another radar facility in Bahrain with drones, which were reportedly intercepted; the United States retaliated with a strike on an Iranian missile launch site on Qeshm Island. Iran responded on Wednesday with an attack on Ali Al Salem air base in Kuwait. There were no reports of damage. Bahrain also said it intercepted Iranian aerial attacks on Wednesday.

Industry observers note that under pressure. U.S. President Donald Trump has been vague about his prepares in the war, and some reports suggest he is mulling over ordering expansive strikes. But Trump on Thursday indicated that he’s not in a hurry to escalate. “I am not rushing into any decision. We will see what happens after the beginning of the year,” Trump told Axios.

Trump’s comments came as Israel is reportedly pressing the White House to escalate with a fresh bombing campaign. Roman Gofman, the director of the Israeli intelligence agency Mossad, visited Washington this week, where he is stated to have expressed concerns to U.S. officials over alleged Iranian chemical weapons development.

The United States also has intelligence that Iran has drawn up plans to potentially use a dirty bomb or chemical weapon in Washington, according to a CNN report. Trump on Tuesday said the United States was looking into the dirty bomb report and takes it “very seriously.” But he later downplayed the prospect of Iran actually using such a weapon in Washington, and he warned that “if it does happen, we’ll wipe them out.” Trump this week also told Fox News there’s “indication that Iran is looking at gasses, looking at bio, because we’ve shut them out with the nuclear.”.

According to recent reports, “And they’re looking at gas and biological weapons. Not nice. And we’ll see,” he noted.

Iran also remains defiant in the face of continued U.S. economic pressure, and Tehran appears emboldened by major Republican losses in the midterm elections.

#100048. America Can Do Good—and Do Well

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2894 w)

America Can Do Good—and Do Well

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2894 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • ANDREW NATSIOS was Administrator of the U.S.
  • Among all the ruinous consequences of the so-called U.S.
  • No country can be a great power without a functioning foreign aid program.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

ANDREW NATSIOS was Administrator of the U.S. Agency for International Development and the President’s Special Envoy to Sudan during the George W. Bush administration. He is the author of Guns Are Not Enough: Foreign Aid in the National Interest, from which this essay is adapted.

The Strategic Logic of Foreign Aid.

Among all the ruinous consequences of the so-called U.S. Department of Government Efficiency’s efforts to cut bureaucracy, none has been as profound as the destruction of the United States’ ability to deliver foreign aid. A comprehensive Lancet study shows that the U.S. Agency for International Development’s assistance prevented more than 90 million deaths between 2001 and 2021. Using a mortality model, Boston University epidemiologist Brooke Nichols has estimated that the 2025 dismantling of USAID contributed to more than 700,000 excess deaths over roughly a year. A study published in Science this May found that after USAID’s shutdown, places that had lost large amounts of the agency’s assistance experienced a marked uptick in armed clashes and riots. The development economists Marcella Nicolini and Fabio Sabatini, meanwhile, demonstrated that economic activity in areas that formerly enjoyed substantial U.S. aid had dramatically declined.

No country can be a great power without a functioning foreign aid program. But today, the United States does not have one. After 90 percent of USAID’s programs were terminated and 90 percent of its staff members were laid off, Congress formally reappropriated most of the budgetary funding dedicated to U.S. foreign aid. But the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) has not released all of this appropriated funding. More damaging still, USAID’s mechanisms for spending aid money have been dismantled. According to the Pew Research Center, annual U.S. foreign aid disbursements fell by $26 billion between the 2023–24 and 2024–25 fiscal years; $2.5 billion in appropriated funding designated for foreign aid went unspent by the end of the 2025–26 fiscal year.

Russell Vought, OMB’s director and a self-identified Christian nationalist, has stonewalled spending for programs related to supporting democracy and insisted that humanitarian grants can be sent only to two specific Christian nongovernmental organizations. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, meanwhile, announced that he wanted to end funding to USAID development contractors, universities, and local civil society organizations without understanding the downside of other options for aid dollars, such as budget support, which are far less accountable, uniquely American, and results-oriented.

Given the suffering created by the end of USAID, it is even more troubling that DOGE’s objectives to slash waste and boost transparency have not been realized. U.S. President Donald Trump’s 2025 “massive beautiful bill” erased any modest savings won by DOGE’s cuts to foreign aid. And the decision to move USAID’s functions to the State Department, which has weak business systems and inadequate staff to manage aid programs, has thus far led to the transfer of $3.8 billion in U.S. foreign aid money to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs and $15.9 billion directly into foreign governments’ treasuries through memorandums of understanding.

Industry observers note that these governments often have limited capacity to spend the money wisely and produce results. In the past, USAID’s Office of the Inspector General has harshly criticized such options because it is nearly impossible to audit the transfers. Over 90 percent of the countries involved in these agreements score below 50 (out of 100) on Transparency International’s Corruption Perceptions Index, indicating serious systemic corruption. This may explain why State Department political appointees have kept the texts of these health agreements secret.

In a recent development, clashing demands—that aid should relieve misery abroad, that it ought to serve U.S. military and diplomatic interests, and that it ought to yield rapid, visible, and quantifiable results—always complicated the enterprise. And over the course of 65 years since USAID’s 1961 founding, overregulation, a centralization of control over programs, and congressional meddling created a rigid straitjacket that made the United States less responsive to local governments and local needs. But what the current U.S. administration didn’t understand was that USAID’s bureaucracy, so often presented as an obstacle to effectiveness, was in fact an adaptation to manage these conflicts.

Simply abolishing that institutional architecture with no blueprint to replace it has only generated more confusion and waste. Meanwhile, China is racing to offer alternative sources of development financing, and Russia is seeking to expand its global influence through security partnerships. The United States cannot afford to let its foreign aid apparatus atrophy. It must redirect it, not reject aid.

Sources indicate that ever since USAID was created, the expectations that leaders in Washington had for foreign aid have conflicted with realities in the developing world, the way actual aid programs are managed, and the speed and nature of societal change. When I read through USAID’s 1960s-era archives to write my fresh book, I was struck that the demands early U.S. policymakers made of the institution were the same as those made today: policymakers wanted rapid, visible, and quantifiable results. Those demands were as unrealistic then as they are now. U.S. President John F. Kennedy hoped that poverty in Latin America would visibly recede within a couple of years of USAID’s creation, as he was understandably worried that the Cuban revolutionary leader Fidel Castro’s Marxist ideology was spreading across the region. Fourteen months after the organization’s inception, an article by Joseph Kraft in Harper’s Magazine reported that policymakers in Washington had already judged it a failure because it was not delivering “quick and visible results.” David Bell, USAID’s second administrator, recalled in 1965 that Kennedy had complained that the agency was “slow-moving, inefficient, and unresponsive to the President’s policy.”.

According to recent reports, but diplomacy and development operate on profoundly different time horizons. Nearly all foreign aid programs have diplomatic consequences, even if they aren’t designed to. When diplomatic goals become the main or only goals of an aid program, however—for instance, when U.S. aid kept the Congolese dictator Mobutu Sese Seko in power during the Cold War—good development often fails.

According to recent reports, the United States began institutionalizing foreign aid after World War II through agencies and programs such as the Marshall Plan, which supported the postwar economic recovery of Western Europe, and the Point Four Program, a Truman administration initiative to promote development in poor countries to reduce their susceptibility to communism. All along, policymakers debated whether U.S. assistance programs should principally aim to save lives and reduce extreme poverty or to support U.S. foreign policy by countering the influence of hostile powers.

Recent findings suggest that in fact, USAID ended up playing a key role in winning the Cold War. American assistance strengthened governments targeted for Soviet and Chinese communist subversion, particularly in Asia. After U.S. President Richard Nixon entered his second year in office, aid spending for agriculture was increased to 50 percent of USAID’s budget and was directed primarily toward Asia. According to multiple studies by development economists, the effort saved more than 245 million lives. The green revolution, implemented over decades in Pakistan, India, Indonesia, the Philippines, South Korea, and Taiwan (among other countries), helped produce large grain surpluses that fueled industrialization and economic growth and averted the kind of famines that historically produce coups or mass uprisings.

Sources indicate that throughout this era, however, Washington’s demands that aid accomplish diplomatic goals—and quickly and visibly—also undermined the most notable elements of development programs: institution building and policy reform. Strong institutions separate wealthy countries from poor ones. The former have them in abundance, while the latter do not. Institution building and policy reform should be the focus of aid programs. But institution building and policy reform is difficult to measure, takes many years to implement successfully, and is not immediately visible. Instead, policymakers insisted that USAID do service delivery, producing valuable humanitarian programs that were ultimately unsustainable.

Most critical analyses of U.S. foreign aid conclude that USAID came to focus on process over substance, resulting in excessive bureaucracy. What these critiques overlook is what caused this obsessive focus on process. A web of federal regulatory and oversight agencies (what scholars call the counterbureaucracy) loosed on U.S. aid programs an army of federal auditors, accountants, regulators, compliance officers, and congressional staffers dedicated to reining in the bureaucracy and—supposedly—protecting taxpayers’ money. This onslaught slowed down USAID’s implementation of programs and created massive amounts of paperwork. It did not make aid programs more effective.

Historically, Congress ended up playing a particularly intrusive role in the management of U.S. foreign aid programs. USAID reported to 14 congressional committees, which often clashed, pulling USAID in different directions and slowing program implementation. (For example, the House and Senate agriculture committees, under the influence of the agriculture lobby, stonewalled efforts to reform food aid by insisting it be exported from the United States, while legislative appropriators and authorizers from foreign affairs committees strongly supported local purchase reform.) Congress also imposed intrusive earmarks—defined amounts allocated for specific programs, projects, or organizations. When countries asked for specific help, USAID often could not respond, because the glut of earmarks meant there was no discretionary money left.

Sources indicate that starting in the 1990s, the State Department attempted to exert more control over the USAID budget. A 1998 statute, for instance, made the USAID administrator report directly to the secretary of state. In January 2001, the State Department took control of USAID’s budget. That only led lawmakers—who often distrusted State—to add more earmarks. To protect U.S. foreign aid programs from an especially hostile Senate Foreign Relations Committee chairman, Republican Senator Jesse Helms, the Clinton administration instructed each cabinet-level department to create its own aid programs that would fall outside that committee’s jurisdiction. For example, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention at the Department of Health and Human Services established regional offices around the world, the Environmental Protection Agency developed solar energy projects in poor countries, and the Federal Emergency Management Agency signed agreements with more than 28 developing countries to assist in disaster management. USAID was already running programs such as these, yielding overlapping mandates which added to the incoherence of U.S. foreign aid.

When I became USAID administrator in 2001, I discovered a foreign aid program whose funds were straitjacketed by nearly 250 congressional earmarks, a sum exceeding USAID’s total appropriation. At the time, Ethiopia was one of the most severely food insecure countries in the world. Yet in 2007 only 1.5 percent of USAID’s budget was devoted to agricultural development, 1.5 percent to economic growth, and 1.5 percent to governance reform; Congressional earmarks made it impossible to fund these programs to match the Ethiopian government’s request.

Recent findings suggest that despite all these impediments, foreign aid remained a critical component of U.S. foreign policy. The Department of Defense had a particularly productive partnership with USAID, recognizing that foreign aid could be as important as force in incentivizing insurgents to make peace. The effects of USAID projects in Afghanistan were profound but took shape over long time horizons neither the State Department nor the Defense Department had any patience for. (USAID’s Afghanistan media-development program, for instance, was a great success, as documented in a Harvard Kennedy School study by The New York Times’s David Rohde.) Major academic studies have shown that in Iraq, community development projects undertaken by USAID’s Office of Transition Initiatives (OTI) employed large numbers of young men who might otherwise have been recruited into militias, reducing U.S. military casualties in the provinces with the highest levels of violence. In 2004, Army General Peter Chiarelli called the USAID officer managing the program, Kirk Day, a “hero” for saving his soldiers’ lives.

The DOGE team abolished OTI last year, along with innumerable other programs that alleviated suffering globally and enhanced U.S. soft power. When Congress restored many cuts to foreign aid, it did not reinstate USAID’s veteran staff, historical archives, business systems, field presence, or implementing partner networks of universities, international nongovernmental organizations, local civil society groups, and international development contractors. The transfer of programs to the Department of State only exacerbated the contradictions that have long bedeviled U.S foreign aid. Few secretaries of state (or secretaries of defense) have any development background, experience, or technical knowledge, and paradoxically, when aid is seen simply as a tool of diplomacy or defense rather than an end in itself, the diplomatic good it can do is compromised.

Dismantling USAID did not abolish the need for technically knowledgeable staff and bureaucratic systems. In May 2025, the State Department inspector general issued an intimidating report detailing what the department will have to do to competently manage foreign aid programs, a list of demands it will have difficulty meeting. And in September this year, the Government Accountability Office issued a highly critical audit of the State Department’s inadequate management of foreign aid programs, finding that the department lacked documented standards for deciding which aid programs to terminate, could not produce data on its own staffing, and maintained incomplete or incorrect records on grants and agreements. This result was unsurprising, given that the State Department is a diplomatic policy institution, not a program management agency. Merging USAID into the State Department makes as much sense as merging Microsoft with ExxonMobil, given the disparate time horizons on which the two institutions operate and their differences in mission statements and business systems.

Industry observers note that the State Department has pursued alternative arrangements for distributing aid that require less direct management. For example, it has negotiated 36 memorandums of understanding with governments in developing countries to transfer U.S. aid funds to their health ministries, so they can spend the program money themselves. But in return for these transfers, Washington has asked these countries to send private health-care data to the U.S. government, accept undocumented immigrants the U.S. government deports, and, in some cases, give U.S. mining companies access to their rare-earth minerals. Because health programs save lives, they should be distributed based on need, not on parochial, transactional American demands.

Many countries have understandably resisted this kind of bargain. USAID had technical staff that could assess a foreign government’s ability to manage funds responsibly. In practice, it ran a detailed and thorough vetting of nearly every aspect of the governments it partnered with. The State Department, by contrast, only vets according to the legal minimum and treats foreign governments as it treats as international or U.S.-based NGOs. State’s approach will increase the risk that funds are stolen by local government ministries that lack the control systems needed to ensure accountability.

Industry observers note that the very public and grossly inaccurate attacks on USAID’s integrity and management by Trump and DOGE’s erstwhile leader, Elon Musk, have damaged the agency’s reputation so extensively that simply resurrecting it will be difficult. But Washington’s aid apparatus also needs more coherent organization than it was afforded in the past. In his celebrated work Bureaucracy, on which my book is structured, the political scientist James Q. Wilson argues that strong U.S. departments or agencies need “relative autonomy”: clearly defined missions they do not substantially share with other agencies. By this logic, if the United States wants a high-functioning, coherent foreign aid program, it must first consolidate all aid functions within one department.

Sources indicate that abolishing field offices (called USAID missions) also made administering aid programs much more difficult, blunted true accountability and U.S. influence in the developing world, and reduced the visibility of U.S. aid programs. These country missions must be reestablished, reporting to the local U.S. ambassador. In Washington, Congress should create a latest cabinet-level department reporting to the president that manages all the government’s aid programs, which would make it possible to trim staff, streamline program implementation, and avoid policy incoherence. At least 80 percent of this new department’s staff should be deployed abroad, not in Washington. The United States will always need to be able to launch aid programs with an expressly diplomatic purpose and short time horizon, and the State Department should determine these projects and their spending levels. But it should leave the programs’ management up to the new aid department—as it did during the Cold War, when USAID was independent of State.

In a recent development, this fresh department should also report to fewer congressional committees—a foreign affairs authorizing committee and an appropriations subcommittee in each legislative body. The practice of burdening the United States’ foreign aid budget with domestically appealing earmarks—which prevents aid from responding to foreign countries’ own needs—must be reduced.

In the past, the overregulation and bureaucratization of foreign aid driven by the demands of the counterbureaucracy prioritized process over programs and compliance over developmental outcomes. The newly introduced aid department must be given regulatory relief. One way to do that is for Congress to set up charter missions, similar to charter schools, as an experiment to see whether accountability deteriorates. These deregulated charter missions would be free from burdensome reporting requirements the counterbureaucracy demands. In recent years, the World Bank has tried a similar approach and found that it improved its programs’ effectiveness without increasing fraud.

Recent findings suggest that the status quo for U.S. foreign aid cannot last. But Washington cannot revert to the old status quo, which generated the kind of dissatisfactions among policymakers that helped lead to its dismantling. Now is the time to bring more coherence to U.S. foreign aid programs with these reforms, if the latest Democratic Congress and future administrations show a forward-looking vision.

Welcome back to Foreign Policy’s Latin America Brief.

The highlights this week: Three regional presidents travel to China, the United States and Venezuela strike a military deal, and the region weighs fossil fuel phaseout looks at COP31.

Welcome back to Foreign Policy’s Latin America Brief.

The highlights this week: Three regional presidents travel to China, the United States and Venezuela strike a military deal, and the region weighs fossil fuel phaseout aims at COP31.

Sources indicate that this week, many observers focused on the trilateral meeting among the presidents of China, Russia, and the United States on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit. Three Latin American presidents were also in Shenzhen, China, for the meetings: those of Chile, Mexico, and Peru.

In a recent development, all six countries are APEC members. Though the bloc’s Latin American leaders don’t always attend the annual summit in person, they did this year—and held separate bilateral meetings with Chinese President Xi Jinping. The 2028 APEC conference, hosted by Mexico, will see Asian leaders travel to Latin America.

In their trips to Shenzhen, the three presidents signaled that they value relations with China despite pressure from the United States to spurn the country.

It has been revealed that the U.S. National Security Strategy issued by the Trump administration last year remarked that allowing “non-Hemispheric competitors” to grow their presence in the Americas was a “strategic mistake.” And the U.S. ambassadors to both Mexico and Peru disparaged China in social media posts this week.

Mexico has applied new tariffs on Chinese goods since U.S. President Donald Trump returned to office, with some as high as 50 percent. But China remains Mexico’s No. 2 trade partner, and Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum remarked in Shenzhen that she hoped her trip would yield more Mexican avocado and tequila exports to China and new cooperation on smart hospitals.

For Mexico, “integration with the United States and market access to the United States is priority No. 1,” remarked Diego Marroquín, a fellow in the Americas program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies. But “they can achieve that and at the same time, they can engage more with China,” he said, especially on complications that aren’t central to U.S. interests.

Sources indicate that in more sensitive areas, such as critical infrastructure and telecommunications, Mexico “will most likely accommodate U.S. demands,” Marroquín wrote this week.

Sources indicate that chile has not imposed tariffs on Chinese goods, though it has seen tensions with China flare in other ways. This month, Chile and Belgium jointly challenged a Chinese bid to permanently host the secretariat of the newly introduced United Nations High Seas Treaty.

The dispute over hosting rights is still unresolved, and Chilean President José Antonio Kast did not mention it in his bilateral meeting with Xi, according to multiple reports. The two countries revealed a upcoming economic cooperation road map without providing specifics. The partnership is potentially promising news for Chile as it experiences a recession.

Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori, meanwhile, walked away with a more concrete commitment from China: a $22.5 million pledge to help Peru deal with the fallout of El Niño. Both countries also celebrated an patch to their free trade deal that took effect this month, which officials noted could help trade and investment rise by streamlining import- and export-related bureaucracy.

It has been revealed that “Our meeting allows us to strengthen relations between Peru and China,” Fujimori wrote on social media after meeting with Xi. The Chinese readout noted that Fujimori praised the majority-Chinese-operated port in the Chancay, Peru—an investment that the Trump administration has criticized.

Fujimori, Kast, and Sheinbaum held additional bilateral meetings at APEC. Sheinbaum met with Trump, while all three Latin American presidents sat down with other Asian leaders, including those of Japan; Vietnam; the Philippines, with which Chile signed a free trade agreement; and Thailand, with which Peru did the same.

It has been revealed that the meetings show that the three leaders hope to deepen ties not only with China but also more broadly with Asia. They are not alone in their neighborhood: Last weekend, Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva addressed the opening session of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit in Manila, Philippines.

Sources indicate that these countries’ trade flows are beginning to reflect the presidential trips. To give one example, Mexico’s total goods traded with Japan between January and September of this year was 9 percent higher than over the same period in 2025, according to Mexican government statistics. With Thailand, trade grew by 50 percent, and with Malaysia, by 78 percent.

Friday, Nov. 20: Fujimori meets Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi in Tokyo.

Sources indicate that monday, Nov. 23, to Friday, Nov. 27: Polish President Karol Nawrocki visits Argentina and Chile.

Thursday, Dec. 3, to Friday, Dec. 4: Uruguay hosts the Mercosur leaders’ summit.

Industry observers note that U.S. military deals. Less than a year after removing Venezuela’s president by force, the United States signed a military partnership with the country’s acting leaders on Wednesday. In Caracas to ink the deal, U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth called Venezuela a “compliant security partner” and mentioned the arrangement would allow both countries to better combat drug gangs.

Former Venezuelan President Hugo Chávez ended Venezuelan military cooperation with the United States in 2005, and his successors in the chavismo movement have used their control over Venezuela’s military apparatus to cling to power and crush dissent.

Rocío San Miguel, a top Venezuelan human rights advocate, told Union Radio that the U.S. partnership could be an opportunity to rein in Venezuela’s military, relegating it to its intended constitutional role.

The Venezuela deal comes as U.S. military cooperation with neighboring Colombia appears to be falling short of Trump’s vision. The New York Times reported on Wednesday that Hegseth altered his travel plans to Colombia this week after the country’s government said it lacked the congressional votes to greenlight U.S. military operations on its soil.

Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella wrote on social media afterward that he did not reject a specific plan but added that any U.S. military cooperation must follow Colombian law.

Shifting regional affinities. A gathering of Latin America scholars and policymakers in Rio de Janeiro last week highlighted the cross-border integration that is often excluded from headlines about the region. This newsletter writer attended the event, Conversatorio Latinoamericano.

Recent findings suggest that one speaker flagged a recent University of Buenos Aires opinion survey about Argentines’ attitudes on geopolitics. Between 2025 and 2026, Brazil surpassed the United States to top respondents’ answers to two questions: “Which country do you think Argentina should have relations with?” and “Which country do you think Argentina should be like?”.

The shift suggests that average Argentines don’t fully embrace President Javier Milei’s pro-Trump pivot—or his chilled relations with Brazil.

It has been revealed that natalia Saltalamacchia Ziccardi of the Mexico Autonomous Institute of Technology said that Brazil and Mexico are turning the page on years of distrust, experiencing a “springtime” of warming ties since around 2024. She cited increased high-level visits, coordination in response to Venezuela’s crisis, and shared support for a Chilean U.N. secretary-general candidate.

These sympathies show that dividing the region into pro- and anti-Trump camps is an oversimplification.

Chilean director Sebastián Lelio, winner of the best foreign language film award for A Fantastic Woman, poses in the press room during the 90th Academy Awards in Hollywood, California, on March 4, 2018.Alberto E. Rodriguez/Getty Images.

Industry observers note that chilean cinema pioneer. This month, Chileans are remembering star film director Sebastián Lelio, who died on Nov. 6 at the age of 52. Lelio got his start as part of a wave of indie Chilean filmmaking in the 2000s that focused on small-scale, interpersonal plotlines and was dubbed Novísimo Cine Chileno by critics.

Lelio’s most beloved works include the 2013 film Gloria, which reveals the ups and downs of dating as a 58-year-old divorcée in the capital of Santiago, and the 2017 film A Fantastic Woman, which follows a transgender singer dealing with the logistics triggered by the death of her partner—and the prejudice that she faces from his conservative family.

A Fantastic Woman won Chile its first-ever Oscar for best foreign language film and helped pave the way for the passage of a 2018 trans rights law. Though Lelio worked across genres, La Tercera’s Gonzalo Valdivia wrote that he “found his natural habitat in portraits of female characters who don’t give in or apologize.”.

Which Latin American country was the first to strike a free trade deal with China?

The two countries signed the agreement in 2005.

Panamanian Environment Minister Juan Carlos Navarro speaks during a press conference discussing electrification at COP31 in Antalya, Turkey, on Nov. 18. Chris McGrath/Getty Images.

Sources indicate that the leaders of Antigua and Barbuda, the Bahamas, Barbados, Bolivia, Brazil, St. Lucia, and Venezuela all traveled to this year’s U.N. climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, known as COP31. The conference is due to wrap up on Friday.

COP31 has moved the ball forward on some initiatives from last year’s U.N. climate summit, which Brazil hosted. For example, a planned investment fund that would pay countries to keep tropical forests intact has now raised more than $8 billion, thanks to a new pledge from Canada.

In a recent development, last week, Brazil published a framework for countries to create national prepares for transitioning away from fossil fuels, a topic that generated buzz at last year’s summit but was cut from the final agreement. Its potential inclusion in the COP31 agreement is still being haggled over.

Industry observers note that while Brazil has left a substantial mark on COP31, so too has a previous Latin American government: that of Colombian President Gustavo Petro, who departed in August. Unsatisfied with last year’s event, the Petro administration hosted a fresh global conference in April that was devoted entirely to quitting fossil fuels, which will see a second edition next year in Tuvalu.

Sources indicate that A group of countries that was heavily involved in planning both conferences has also committed to creating a binding treaty on moving away from fossil fuels. Though Colombia has stayed quiet about the fossil fuel treaty initiative under de la Espriella, countries including Guatemala and Panama had joined it by the time that COP31 arrived.

“We are being held hostage by the petroleum mafia,” Panamanian Environment Minister Juan Carlos Navarro stated at COP31.

It has been revealed that many Latin American countries are at the moment led by right-wing leaders who have not styled themselves as climate champions. But they are nevertheless moving forward on an matter that has been proposed as a main outcome of COP31: electrification.

This year, Brazil is on track to more than double the number of electric vehicles, or EVs, sold since last year, while Mexico’s EV sales are up by more than 25 percent. Countries across the region are planning large-scale battery storage build-outs to support larger electric grids.

The attractive price of green energy—and its insulation from global price shocks—is keeping the region’s green transition gradually moving forward.

Catherine Osborn is the writer of Foreign Policy’s weekly Latin America Brief. She is a print and radio journalist based in Rio de Janeiro. X: @cculbertosborn.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Incoming Democratic leaders called for tighter semiconductor export controls and investigations of the Trump administration Monday as Nvidia reinstated disgraced CEO Jensen Huang.
  • The issue also spilled into the party’s Senate majority leader election fight, as Democrats weigh aims to advance bills in the 120th Congress that would regulate artificial intelligence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., is among Democrats looking to take a harder line on AI and chip exports in the latest year. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo).

Incoming Democratic leaders called for tighter semiconductor export controls and investigations of the Trump administration Monday as Nvidia reinstated disgraced CEO Jensen Huang.

The issue also spilled into the party’s Senate majority leader election fight, as Democrats weigh aims to advance bills in the 120th Congress that would regulate artificial intelligence.

The reinstatement of Huang came as President Donald Trump told CNBC on Monday the CEO “did nothing wrong” and that he had been “speaking to the [Nvidia] board directly and indirectly.”.

It has been revealed that in a Monday statement, Nvidia remarked its board had “received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.”.

Industry observers note that sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., who is challenging Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., for the majority leader role, told reporters Monday that in the “first 100 days” of the newly introduced Congress, he wants Senate rules changed to allow for faster floor consideration of bills that had broad bipartisan support in committee.

He also supports legislation to require independent mandatory evaluations of AI systems and updates to liability laws to account not just for harm caused by AI models but for risks of internal development. He also mentioned a bill he sponsored that he stated would ensure other electricity consumers don’t bear the costs of data center construction.

Van Hollen also stated that Congress should create a special joint committee on AI to consider the technology’s broader impacts, including on the workforce and economy.

“I think we need to move urgently on the safety piece and then move with deliberation, but also speed, on tackling these other issues,” Van Hollen noted.

Industry observers note that last week, Sen. John Hickenlooper, D-Colo., wrote to Van Hollen and Schumer proposing a joint committee to “complement” the work of committees of jurisdiction and asking for their plans for AI if they were elected leader.

Sources indicate that speaking to reporters and in his reply to Hickenlooper, Van Hollen also supported greater transparency into the AI industry’s financing and debt structure and tighter export controls on advanced chips like those sold by Nvidia. In particular, he said the Commerce Department should close “loopholes” for remote access to chips and purchase by affiliates of companies banned from directly acquiring sensitive technologies.

Schumer, in a post on X Monday, said Democrats would “work on a bipartisan basis to continue advancing policies that stop the flow of our most powerful technology to the Chinese military and other adversaries.”.

“Democrats will wield their full power to investigate any wrongdoing by the Trump Administration, Jensen Huang, other NVIDIA executives, and anyone selling out our national security for financial gain,” Schumer wrote.

In a recent development, house Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., whose caucus officially backed him last week to be speaker in the new year, seconded the need for investigations into Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. He also supported export controls.

“The National Defense Authorization Act must include ironclad export control legislation to prevent powerful AI technology from being exploited by the Chinese Communist Party and other adversaries,” Jeffries wrote, referring to the pending fiscal 2027 defense policy bill.

According to recent reports, A manager’s amendment to the Senate’s version of the bill includes several chip export restrictions, including requirements for chip security mechanisms that would allow for verification if semiconductors are diverted to countries of concern and a ban on exporting certain very powerful chips to those countries. The House-passed NDAA does not contain similar language.

Meanwhile, Republican committee leaders pressed forward with prepares to bring in Huang for questioning.

Senate Banking Chair Tim Scott, R-S.C., on Monday confirmed plans for a Dec. 3 hearing titled “Protecting America’s AI Advantage: Oversight of U.S. Export Controls” featuring Huang as a witness.

It has been revealed that "Mr. Huang’s testimony before the Senate Banking Committee will be critical for protecting America’s AI advantage,” Scott stated in a statement. “The national security concerns and adherence to export controls will be central to the committee’s oversight and the congressional hearing.".

Scott previously invited Lutnick to testify before the committee on Dec. 10.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., who looks likely to hold the banking gavel next Congress, noted Huang’s return as CEO “only increases the urgency” of export controls.

“The reckless decision to bring Jensen Huang back as CEO does not change the fact that Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and the organization’s board still owe Congress answers about the company’s compliance with U.S. export controls,” Warren said in a statement.

In a recent development, house Foreign Affairs Chairman Brian Mast, R-Fla., remarked in a social media video on Monday that Huang and Nvidia’s general counsel Tim Teter would sit for transcribed interviews with his committee and with the House Intelligence Committee and Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party the week of Nov. 30.

The committees also requested that Commerce Undersecretary for Industry and Security Jeffrey Kessler appear before the panels.

Tech Report: The Case for a Trump-Xi-Putin Summit

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2680 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that CHARLES KUPCHAN is Professor of International Affairs at Georgetown University and a Senior Fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations.
  • Industry observers note that in just a few days’ time, U.S.
  • Industry observers note that these worries are entirely justified; Trump has a track record of cozying up to autocrats and turning his back on democratic allies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that CHARLES KUPCHAN is Professor of International Affairs at Georgetown University and a Senior Fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations. He is the author of Bringing Order to Anarchy: Governing the World to Come.

Industry observers note that in just a few days’ time, U.S. President Donald Trump, Chinese leader Xi Jinping, and Russian President Vladimir Putin could be holding a three-way summit on the sidelines of next week’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meeting in Shenzhen, China. According to The Wall Street Journal, Putin floated the idea of a trialogue last month as an opportunity to discuss ending the war in Ukraine. No firm plan has yet been announced, but even the prospect of this meeting has provoked widespread consternation. Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski warned against a repeat of the Yalta Conference of 1945, when U.S. President Franklin Roosevelt and British Prime Minister Winston Churchill capitulated to Soviet leader Joseph Stalin’s push for the Soviet Union to dominate Eastern Europe. U.S. Senator Chris Coons posted on X that “there can be no talks about Ukraine’s future without Ukraine at the table, and there can be no real negotiations as long as Trump signals weakness and servitude to Xi and Putin at every opportunity.”.

Industry observers note that these worries are entirely justified; Trump has a track record of cozying up to autocrats and turning his back on democratic allies. Should he sit down with Xi and Putin, he must avoid selling out European and Asian partners who will not be at the table. And given the three leaders’ headstrong personalities and competing national interests that pit the United States against what Xi calls a “no limits” partnership between China and Russia, the meeting might ultimately yield little progress on major issues.

In a recent development, nevertheless, Trump would be right to join a summit with Xi and Putin. No U.S. president has ever held a trilateral meeting with the leaders of China and Russia, and the proposed talks would break the ice and begin to normalize much-needed dialogue. Authoritarianism is not going away, so autocracies and democracies must learn not only to live comfortably alongside one another but also to work together to tame geopolitical rivalry and tackle global challenges in an interdependent world. Americans will not find it easy to get along with the likes of Russia and China, whose political systems threaten the U.S. commitment to spreading democracy. But Trump is taking a bold step in the right direction by engaging with the heads of the world’s leading autocracies.

If he meets with Xi and Putin, Trump should aim low and focus on making meaningful, if limited, progress on a small number of core complications that could benefit from a three-way conversation: the flash points of the Korean Peninsula, Ukraine, and Iran, as well as arms control and strategic stability. But even if the summit yields no concrete results, it will nonetheless have been worthwhile. Trump, Xi, and Putin are paving the way for their successors to advance great-power cooperation across ideological lines and stabilize a fragmented world.

In a recent development, I have argued previously, including in a 2021 Foreign Affairs essay with Richard Haass, that a global concert—an informal steering group of great powers modeled on the nineteenth-century Concert of Europe—offers the best hope of curbing geopolitical competition and enabling collective action in a multipolar world. In addition to the United States, China, and Russia, a upcoming concert would include India, Japan, the European Union, and representatives from Africa, Latin America, the Middle East, and Southeast Asia. Concerts sacrifice representation for efficacy and give only the geopolitically influential states that must be there a seat at the table. They set aside ideological differences and bring democracies and autocracies together to focus on international cooperation. Because concerts eschew binding, enforceable procedures in favor of informal consensus building, they can succeed when formal institutions such as the UN Security Council are paralyzed and when the United States wavers in its commitment to rules-based multilateralism.

But the time has not come for a global concert. Concerts function effectively only when their members are committed to the territorial status quo, are willing to exercise strategic restraint and pursue mutual benefits, and are ready to settle disputes diplomatically. Putin’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine and Xi’s decision to back Russia have, for now, scuttled hopes that the great powers will normalize restraint and the peaceful settlement of disputes. Meanwhile, Trump’s “America first” statecraft shuns joint action and mutual gain in favor of unilateralism.

Yet even though Trump, Xi, and Putin are the wrong leaders at the wrong time to establish a great-power steering group that other major players would eventually join, Trump’s iconoclastic diplomacy sets a useful precedent. His Alaska summit with Putin last year and two summits with Xi this year were admittedly long on pageantry and short on substance. But by taking the controversial step of pursuing joint talks with the two leaders, Trump is widening the diplomatic Overton window and expanding what is politically possible for future U.S. presidents. Avoiding great-power conflict and taming a world in increasing disarray requires the United States to build constructive relations with both China and Russia. Trump deserves credit for starting a trialogue that his successors can carry forward.

If they meet in Shenzhen, Trump, Xi, and Putin should focus on easing tensions at key geopolitical flash points. The Korean Peninsula presents the best opportunity for the three leaders to collaborate. At the UN General Assembly in September, South Korean President Lee Jae-myung laid out an ambitious proposal for normalizing relations with Pyongyang, including a proposal to replace the peninsula’s 1953 armistice with a “peace regime” that promotes “respect for each other’s systems and acknowledgement of our differences.” As part of that plan, Lee has advocated a phased approach to North Korean denuclearization, with an initial freeze on weapons development followed by gradual reductions in Pyongyang’s arsenal of nuclear weapons and ballistic missiles until the peninsula is denuclearized.

Lee’s bold proposal could bring U.S., Chinese, and Russian interests into alignment. Trump has made it clear that he wants to de-escalate tensions on the Korean Peninsula and is already seeking a meeting with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. Beijing and Moscow are competing for influence over Kim, but both want a stable relationship between North and South Korea, so they might be willing to cooperate on proposals to halt nuclear weapons production and encourage talks between Pyongyang and Seoul. Trump, Xi, and Putin should aim to emerge from their meeting with a plan for advancing Lee’s peace agenda; jointly supporting a freeze on North Korean nuclear weapons development is a good place to start.

The prospects for progress toward ending the war in Ukraine are much dimmer but not nonexistent. Trump should be striving to weaken Russia’s ability to sustain the war, but he has long resisted tightening sanctions on Moscow. He talks up potential business ventures with Russia and, in recent weeks, even struck a deal with Putin to get more Russian diesel into global markets and waived a fresh round of congressional sanctions against Moscow. Trump evidently cares more about trying to bring down fuel prices than about curbing Russia’s ability to fund its war against Ukraine.

A summit offers Trump the opportunity to change course and try to convince Xi to restrain Putin. Trump has vowed to bring the war in Ukraine to an end, and the Chinese leader can help him achieve that goal. Xi has enormous leverage over Putin: China backs the Kremlin diplomatically, is the largest buyer of Russian oil and gas, and is the main supplier of dual-use items such as semiconductors and machine tools that are critical to Russian weapons manufacturing.

Recent findings suggest that xi has played along with Putin’s war against Ukraine so far, presumably because the conflict diverts U.S. attention and resources away from Asia, divides NATO, and allows Xi and Putin to cast themselves as leading a global resistance to Western hegemony. But when Xi and Trump met this May, the leaders agreed to pursue “a constructive relationship of strategic stability” between China and the United States, which Xi could advance by pressing Putin to de-escalate. As more Russians feel the effects of the war, the Kremlin may be newly receptive to such pressure. Ukrainian drone strikes are taking a significant toll on Russia’s oil sector and logistics networks, which means Russian citizens face mounting gas and commodities shortages. Meanwhile, some 35,000 Russian soldiers per month are losing their lives or sustaining severe injuries in eastern Ukraine, forcing Putin to consider the unpopular move of ramping up military mobilization. With no battlefield victory in sight, Putin has reasons to entertain a diplomatic off-ramp.

In a recent development, trump and Xi could press Putin to accept a set of limited but consequential steps to de-escalate the conflict. These could include an agreement between Russia and Ukraine—brokered and monitored by Washington and Beijing—to end attacks on energy installations and infrastructure, civilian targets, and commercial shipping. Trump and Xi could also jointly press Putin to refrain from actions that could broaden the war, such as penetrating NATO airspace with Russian drones, sabotaging European infrastructure, and threatening to use nuclear weapons. This pressure, combined with the allure of improving diplomatic and commercial ties to the United States, might convince Putin to relent on at least some of these problems.

Recent findings suggest that trump could also use a trilateral summit to seek help extricating the United States from its war in Iran—a quagmire that has produced regional mayhem and soaring oil prices. As Tehran continues to issue maximalist demands and the war disrupts shipping through the straits of Hormuz and Bab el Mandeb, Trump needs an out.

Sources indicate that neither Xi nor Putin has yet been inclined to lend a hand. China is still buying Iranian oil and providing Tehran with military intelligence and dual-use items that end up in Iranian drones and missiles, and Russia is providing satellite targeting data, munitions, advanced drone technology, and logistical support. Both Beijing and Moscow are happy to see the United States mired in a conflict that is exacerbating divisions within the American electorate and fracturing NATO.

As a major energy exporter, Russia benefits from the spike in oil prices that the conflict has triggered, so pressing Putin to cease supporting Iran is likely a lost cause. But China is the world’s largest oil importer, and Beijing has a vested interest in lowering energy prices by stabilizing exports from the Middle East. Although China’s large oil reserves have buffered its economy from rising oil prices so far, those reserves have been significantly depleted. China’s crude oil imports have begun to climb again, leaving its economy exposed to high energy prices if the conflict drags on. And as the world’s largest exporter of goods, China suffers from the dampening effect high energy prices have on global growth.

It has been revealed that xi might therefore be amenable to helping Trump end the war. Trump should ask Xi to stop or at least slow the flow of Chinese dual-use items to Iran. Washington’s naval blockade and financial and commercial sanctions on Tehran have already taken a toll on Iran’s economy and military supply chains. By cutting off Chinese technology shipments to Iran, Beijing could deepen this economic isolation and help convince Tehran to negotiate an end to the conflict.

Xi could also press Iran to drop its unrealistic demands for ending the war, including that the United States withdraw its forces from the Gulf, release frozen Iranian assets, and remove economic sanctions. Washington might well be willing to offer economic relief, but only as part of postwar negotiations toward a deal that reins in Iran’s nuclear ambitions. Xi could help clear the way for those talks by urging Iran to accept credible terms for ending the immediate conflict.

Beyond working to resolve current conflicts, Trump should promote future strategic stability by pursuing arms control negotiations with Xi and Putin. Every arms control agreement negotiated between Washington and Moscow has expired; their final nuclear pact, Upcoming START, ended in February. There are presently no caps on the American and Russian strategic arsenals and no regular inspections, data exchanges, or notifications of nuclear exercises. This nuclear free-for-all is particularly dangerous given Russia’s nuclear saber rattling amid the war in Ukraine and the Kremlin’s fondness for provocations such as sending explosive-laden drones into NATO airspace.

Sources indicate that in October, Trump appropriately proposed that a trilateral summit include a discussion of nuclear arms control. China has long resisted engaging in arms control talks, arguing that it should not have to limit its nuclear program when its arsenal is much smaller than that of the United States and Russia. But Beijing is rapidly expanding and modernizing its nuclear arsenal. The Pentagon has projected that China will possess more than 1,000 operational warheads by 2030, putting it in nearly the same league as the United States and Russia, which have stockpiles of roughly 1,800 operational warheads each. With the uncertain trajectory of U.S.-Chinese relations, instability on the Korean Peninsula, and China’s tense relationship with Taiwan heightening the risk of conflict in East Asia, Beijing must be part of high-level nuclear arms control discussions.

Realistically, Trump can do little more than start this conversation and invite Xi and Putin to continue it in future trilateral negotiations led by teams of diplomats and arms control experts. In future talks, the three countries should discuss not only caps on nuclear weapons stockpiles but also military-to-military contacts, crisis management protocols, notifications of military exercises, counterproliferation, and other measures that can contribute to strategic stability.

Sources indicate that trump could add a host of other topics to the summit’s agenda, including trade, energy security, and AI regulation, but he should avoid a wide-ranging conversation that goes nowhere. He might, however, notch an easy win by proposing a three-way initiative in an area in which cooperation is relatively straightforward—for example, a joint medical mission to the Democratic Republic of the Congo to help fight Ebola or a joint aid operation to deliver humanitarian relief to Gaza or Yemen. A concrete, public effort along these lines would show that trilateral dialogue can yield viable cooperation.

It has been revealed that yet Trump should guard against being so eager for a win that he lets Xi and Putin take advantage of him. The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit takes place only two weeks after American voters dealt Trump and his party a historic rebuke in the U.S. midterm elections. The notoriously thin-skinned president could be tempted to make concessions to Beijing and Moscow to score a foreign policy breakthrough. He must avoid making a behind-closed-doors compromise on Ukraine that he then tries to force on Kyiv and its European supporters. Similarly, he must hold the line on Taiwan even as he seeks Xi’s help on North Korea, Ukraine, and Iran. Otherwise, Trump will leave the trilateral meeting confirming the worst fears of those who foresaw a new Yalta in the making. Capitulating to Xi and Putin would alienate Washington’s allies, project American weakness, and erode global deterrence.

Recent findings suggest that trump must also carefully manage the optics of a trilateral summit. Putin is an indicted war criminal who continues to prosecute a ruthless war of aggression against Ukraine. It is far too soon to let him out of the penalty box. And although Washington is right to seek a good working relationship with Beijing, it is time for Trump’s “truly great friendship” with Xi to bear fruit. Trump must approach talks with sobriety and pragmatism, seeking to demonstrate that Washington, Beijing, and Moscow can work together to help promote global peace and stability.

Industry observers note that A summit next week will not usher in a newly introduced era of great-power collaboration anytime soon. It might not even yield concrete deliverables. Still, the meeting would set a valuable precedent. Simply by sitting down with Xi and Putin, Trump would begin a much-needed trilateral conversation.
