Avoiding Colombia’s Escalation Trap

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3360 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • ELIZABETH DICKINSON is Deputy Director for Latin America at International Crisis Group.
  • How a U.S.-Backed Offensive Could Help Bogotá Reclaim Its Conflict Zones.
  • Sources indicate that on September 21, José Luis Pérez Villanueva, better known as “El Cholo”—the second-in-command and financial architect of the criminal group Autodefensas Conquistadores de la Sierra Nevada—was killed during a Colombian police operation on the rural outskirts of Santa Marta.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

ELIZABETH DICKINSON is Deputy Director for Latin America at International Crisis Group.

How a U.S.-Backed Offensive Could Help Bogotá Reclaim Its Conflict Zones.

Sources indicate that on September 21, José Luis Pérez Villanueva, better known as “El Cholo”—the second-in-command and financial architect of the criminal group Autodefensas Conquistadores de la Sierra Nevada—was killed during a Colombian police operation on the rural outskirts of Santa Marta. Within hours, militants from that organization released a dramatic campaign of terror. The group, known colloquially as Los Pachenca, demanded that businesses across the city shutter. Some 90 percent of shops did, as videos circulated of gunmen shooting up storefronts that stayed open.

For two decades, Los Pachenca has been the unquestioned criminal authority in the beachfront city and the adjacent Sierra Nevada mountain range, charging extortion payments from businesses and residents and controlling the flow of drugs out of the Port of Santa Marta, en route to Europe and beyond. But the level of control the group exhibited during the strike was particularly jarring, given that Santa Marta is the vacation home of many of the country’s elite and a common destination for international visitors. Colombia’s government responded by militarizing the city, sending in hundreds of soldiers and police officers, who rolled into town on the main highway with tanks and air support. Many shops still stayed closed until the morning of September 25, when the group announced that it was ending the strike. For locals, Los Pachenca’s reaction was a message about who remains in charge.

Calm has since returned to Santa Marta, but the incident may be indicative of risks to come. Colombia’s newly elected president, Abelardo de la Espriella, has promised a steep military escalation against illegal groups, which have grown precipitously in recent years. As he does so, armed and criminal organizations will undoubtedly respond. Often, their target will not be the state. Instead, they will likely direct their violence against the civilian populations, whom they have spent years coopting and coercing. That is because armed and criminal groups across the country have learned that their true leverage is their ability to govern local communities—and to intimidate and punish them into silence. Even when they do attack state forces, their use of weapons such as improvised explosives and makeshift drones means that bystanders often suffer. In one recent incident in the Pacific coast department of Valle del Cauca, four drone attacks debuted by an armed group in a single day left five civilians injured.

Recent findings suggest that these dangers are particularly acute as de la Espriella’s pledge of a zero-tolerance crackdown against armed and criminal groups has won enthusiastic support from Washington. Both countries want substantial and visible victories against these outfits. They triumphantly revealed a latest era of cooperation when the president took office in August, including a promise of upgraded military ties. (The United States has not yet publicly pledged new weapons, but it is already providing greater intelligence and logistical assistance on some operations.) After two years of tensions and threats between President Donald Trump and leftist former President Gustavo Petro, the political realignment means that Colombia is once again the United States’ closest defense ally in South America. This is likely to continue, despite major Democratic wins in the U.S. Congress, as the relationship’s focus on security has a long history of bipartisan support.

According to recent reports, this week, during U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s visit to Bogotá, the de la Espriella administration signaled that it would seek congressional approval for joint military operations with the United States in Colombia. This cooperation will likely yield initial results. The Colombian government has stated that it aims to ramp up attacks against armed and criminal groups and to go after leaders who enjoyed protection as counterparts in peace talks during the past administration.

Yet Colombia’s true challenge is not how to carry out attacks but what to do afterward. Surgical strikes, which see the military enter and exit swiftly, leave civilians more vulnerable in the aftermath, as armed groups retaliate against alleged informants and tighten their grip in areas they control. Bogotá must ensure that every operation includes contingencies to anticipate criminal groups’ reactions and build on successful offensives by weakening their grasp on communities. The government will need to strengthen the police’s ability to patrol contested areas, a costly but necessary process that the United States and other partners should support.

Sources indicate that the stakes are high. Bogotá has a chance to leverage its increased military pressure to open the door for the state, rewriting the story of who governs conflict areas. If the government misses this opportunity to consolidate state control, however, Colombia risks entering an escalatory spiral in which civilians pay a mounting price for a campaign intended to protect them.

Sources indicate that armed and criminal groups have spent the last decade expanding their reach across Colombia. According to the local think tank Pares, the number of municipalities with an armed group presence rose from 212 in 2018 to 518 last year—or about half of all municipalities. This deterioration reversed dramatic and hard-won improvements in security. After the historically violent decades of the 1990s and 2000s, military pressure and negotiations yielded a 2016 peace agreement demobilizing the former Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC), once the country’s dominant rebel group. Colombia’s countryside breathed a sigh of relief as the FARC pulled out of areas where it had been in control, which represented a quarter of the country’s land.

The FARC’s exit, however, did not pave the way for Colombia’s highly centralized and bureaucratic state to claim control of those vast geographies. Instead, old armed groups such as the National Liberation Army and newer ones such as the Gaitanista Army of Colombia (also known as the Gulf Clan) saw a chance to expand their access to trafficking routes, coca crops, illegal mines, and, ultimately, vulnerable rural populations. Kidnapping for extortion and mass displacement began to resurface, shattering optimism that progress would move in one direction. Over the last four years, membership in illegal groups has nearly doubled, to some 27,000 fighters today.

As a candidate, de la Espriella successfully harnessed public frustration by promising mano dura, or iron-fisted tactics, including aerial attacks and increased incarceration, facilitated by the construction of mega-prisons. He blamed his predecessor’s administration for accelerating insecurity. The first leftist to be elected president in modern Colombia, Petro had entered office in 2022 vowing to de-emphasize the military’s role and instead hold peace talks with various armed organizations. But not every group participated, and many of the ones that did sought to take advantage of cease-fires to cement their control over communities. Midway through his term, Petro pivoted back toward deploying the armed forces. But much of the harm was already done.

Colombia’s new president has been in office only a little more than 100 days, but the shift is marked. De la Espriella carried out three bombing raids in his first weeks. He has extradited dozens of individuals to the United States, including senior leaders, and the administration has killed or captured many others. The president is doggedly pushing to restart aerial fumigation of coca crops, which the state carried out in the early 2000s to try to reduce the number of hectares under cultivation; the practice has since been heavily restricted by court rulings over concerns about health and environmental consequences. Both in private and in public, military leaders laud the government’s new support for their operations.

Recent findings suggest that the Trump administration has also welcomed these developments, which align with a regional trend favoring Washington’s approach on counternarcotics. For Colombia, the fresh era of security cooperation with the United States represents a return to the status quo ante of the last quarter century, which was briefly disrupted by the Petro administration. U.S.-Colombian military ties were forged through antidrug efforts and deepened in 1999 with Proposal Colombia, a decadelong $10 billion aid package that funded, among other things, the expansion and professionalization of the security forces and fumigation. The Colombian police and military are deeply integrated with their American counterparts. They use U.S.- and NATO-compatible systems, travel by the hundreds to the United States each year for instruction, and receive American intelligence. In nearly every operation, at least one step (and often far more) in the logistical chain is either coordinated with Washington or relies on U.S. support. That relationship never fully stopped under Petro, but the two sides were notably wary of each other. Now bilateral trust appears to be restored.

Even before the elections, de la Espriella impressed U.S. officials by outlining his plans to reclaim security momentum for the state. The Colombian president is now acting on several explicit U.S. priorities, including extraditions and legislation to designate numerous groups as terrorist organizations. Meanwhile, Bogotá’s coca eradication targets are even more ambitious than Washington’s. At a personal level, relations are strong, too. Two of Colombia’s top military officials previously served as envoys to U.S. Southern Command.

Bogotá claims that it intends to deliver results for Washington’s antidrug goals and has explicitly asked for additional support in the form of funding, aircraft, surveillance technologies, and maintenance. Although Colombia’s military remains among the best trained in the region, its logistical needs are critical. Only 13 of Colombia’s 53 Black Hawk helicopters are in working order, and defense spending has shrunk as a share of the national government’s budget, from 22.4 percent in 2003 to just 14.7 percent in 2025, with a growing proportion of those funds spent on salaries and pensions.

Industry observers note that how much the United States will provide remains to be seen. In August, U.S. Southern Command’s General Francis Donovan discussed ways to shore up the deteriorating air fleet during a visit to Bogotá. The United States has also redeployed surveillance drones from Africa to Colombia and Ecuador, where they are already aiding intelligence collection. But Secretary of State Marco Rubio was reluctant to pledge specific aid while in Colombia in September, and most of this assistance is likely to be in kind or to stay in the hands of the U.S. military and contractors, with little entering the Colombian budget. Much of it appears to be focused on short-term offensive wins.

Recent findings suggest that colombia has returned to tactics such as aerial bombardment because they arguably worked against the FARC. Founded as a Marxist rebellion in the 1960s, the group behaved like a conventional army, dressed in uniforms, and sought out combat with the state. This meant that the Colombian military could bomb encampments and that capturing leaders left the organization at times rudderless. Slowly chipping away at the FARC’s hierarchy and control helped push the group to finally negotiate its disarmament, beginning in 2012.

In a recent development, but today, those same strategies are yielding diminishing returns. The current generation of armed and criminal groups has little interest in confronting the state. Instead, they behave like businesses, seeking to safeguard access to natural resources, supply chains, and trafficking routes. They live within the civilian population and rarely wear uniforms. Leaders are easily replaced and hierarchies are fluid. Critically, Colombia’s armed groups have learned that wars with the military are costly but that controlling local populations—through intimidation and violence, but also by offering economic incentives, jobs, and services—is comparatively cheap. The battlefield has evolved from a conventional conflict to a contest over who can govern territories and the people living there.

Santa Marta offers an example of how this upcoming model of warfare works. On most days, an outsider in the city would never perceive the presence of Los Pachenca. The group’s members do not patrol or identify themselves. Yet residents know them well from the weekly or monthly extortion payments they are forced to make. Local companies and government officials essentially view the group as an inescapable reality. Pushing back carries a violent price, but paying a protection tax, taking a bribe, or facilitating illegal commerce keeps business running smoothly.

It has been revealed that the criminal governance of rural areas is even more suffocating. Groups that emerged from splinters of the former FARC, known as dissidents, often force local residents to hold identity cards, issued so that militants have a full census of who lives in the area and can detect possible enemy fighters. In the Amazon region, these groups keep a land registry more complete than that of the state so that they know exactly whom and how much to extort.

According to recent reports, with this intense surveillance over society, armed and criminal groups frequently deploy the civilian population as human shields against military offensives and police patrols. The most egregious example is the widespread use of forcibly recruited children as bodyguards for senior commanders. De la Espriella’s initial bombardments, which killed at least six children, were even temporarily halted by a court over concerns about minors. Senior officers admit that these types of casualties are inevitable around high-value targets, and that the groups know that the military is far less likely to proceed if it means killing children.

Recent findings suggest that armed and criminal groups will also try to use the military operations to their political advantage. When children are killed in bombardments, for example, FARC dissidents spin the local narrative into a story about how the state cares little for rural populations. The argument sticks because there is rarely a credible state presence that can serve and protect these same communities and earn their trust.

There are more immediate consequences, as well. In the aftermath of bombardments and high-level captures, armed and criminal groups often undertake what amounts to a purge of the population, killing or exiling anyone they believe to have collaborated with the state. And when the state takes out a leader, intra-group violence frequently ensues as former associates compete to take his place. Many residents shelter inside to avoid being caught up in the fighting, leaving children without school and parents without income. If new splinter groups emerge, the combat for control over neighborhoods can place even more civilians in the crossfire. This fallout widens the gap between immediate tactical results and long-term security gains. Taking out a senior leader wins applause, but conditions may well worsen on the ground.

It has been revealed that de la Espriella’s administration has rightly identified winning territorial control, permanently dislodging criminal groups, and restoring state governance as its ultimate goals. The dilemma it now faces—exacerbated by U.S. support that focuses on attention-grabbing wins—is how to both achieve short-term results and ensure that these do not unleash fresh waves of violence, retaliation against civilians, and, in turn, criminal consolidation.

The challenge is twofold. First, the military needs to anticipate groups’ violent reactions and to safeguard the population. In the case of Santa Marta, for example, the government could have increased police presence in the city in the hours after El Cholo was killed. Before the next bombardment or high-level capture, the state should ensure that a ground team of soldiers or military police is ready to hold the ground, protect the community, and prevent the armed group from swiftly stepping back in to reclaim territory.

According to recent reports, the second challenge—establishing lasting territorial control—is trickier. A permanent rural security presence might offer the best chance for Colombia’s government to change the direction of the conflict. The country’s military leadership controls only the tip of the spear, not the rest of the state. Time and again, governments “send only the military to the hardest areas,” a retired senior officer told Crisis Group. Moreover, soldiers are operating under heavy pressure for quick wins, which are measured in the number of combatants and especially high-value targets that are killed or captured. There is a real risk that by focusing largely on these statistics, the state will overlook more comprehensive policies necessary to achieve durable security.

Pressure to deliver fast results has in the past incentivized unacceptable practices. In the early 2000s, intense political demands for combat kills fueled elaborate schemes in which soldiers murdered thousands of civilians and counted them as guerrilla fatalities, a scandal known as “false positives.” These crimes deeply compromised public trust in the security forces, and the military has worked for years to build a culture and procedures that ensure they do not happen again. Today, the country’s senior military leadership is likely the first and best brake on any attempts to use excessive force. Commanders say that they are cognizant of the need to guard against rules being slowly stretched until they are broken. “We need a stronger security approach, but it also worries us when we hear there is pressure for ‘results,’” one officer said. But U.S. rhetoric and behavior, including its decision to sink what it claims are drug-smuggling boats on the high seas, compound these risks.

In a recent development, success, then, may demand a strategy that is ultimately anchored in a much stronger and larger police force, fit for the job of safeguarding civilians rather than merely carrying out offensive strikes. Military operations can generate a window of opportunity by shuffling dynamics on the ground or removing certain dangerous players. Yet those reconfigurations will turn out in the state’s favor only if the resulting vacuum is eventually filled by reliable law enforcement. Take, for example, an operation that temporarily dislodges a group from a rural hamlet. If the military acts alone, it will likely enter and leave in a matter of days or even hours, allowing the armed group to quickly return. If, however, the offensive is followed up with permanent police patrols, access to the justice system, and social interventions, criminals will have a harder time regaining control.

According to recent reports, this, of course, is easier noted than done, given the government’s resource constraints. To create effective and permanent patrols, police departments operating in the countryside need more officers and equipment to maintain a presence in the most remote communities. Colombia has roughly 180,000 uniformed police officers, a figure that, per capita, puts it on the lower end of OECD countries, many of which are far more urbanized and therefore easier to patrol. In Colombia’s conflict-affected areas, outgunned officers must often stay inside their local stations for their own safety, limiting their ability to build trust and channels of communication with the population. Other state institutions, such as the justice system, say that they cannot establish a durable foothold in villages without guarantees of protection in the medium term—exactly what rural policing should strive to provide. The U.S. State Department’s Bureau of International Narcotics and Law Enforcement Affairs has funded the building and equipping of rural police stations in the past; it should expand this work. International partners with long-standing expertise in rural policing, such as Canada and France, could provide critical support, as well.

In cities, the challenge is different. In Santa Marta, for example, the state is present, but it is weak and vulnerable to the pressure and cooptation of the same groups that it must confront. The police need both more officers and better working conditions—including salaries, benefits, access to education, and social support for families—that could help them resist bribes. Regular vetting and counterintelligence checks can help ensure that police are fighting on the side of the state and not its adversaries.

Industry observers note that expanding the police will be an expensive, long-term undertaking. In the interim, Colombia could prioritize more personnel for critical areas and ensure that officers have a strong grounding in community policing, allowing them to understand the most pressing risks facing civilians. That means regular outreach to communities to build trust and make certain that officers are seen as having a stake in local well-being. The United States, meanwhile, must continue to help Bogotá strengthen its police and courts with direct financial and technical assistance.

According to recent reports, colombia, backed by renewed U.S. support, cannot afford to repeat past mistakes or ignore how the conflict has changed. Bogotá must therefore plan for and capitalize on military pressure to do something no government in Colombia’s history has done: govern well in conflict areas.

Ukraine’s Energy Initiative Was Too Little, Too Late

  • Government officials and most analysts in Ukraine concur that renewables and nuclear will underpin the country’s energy and national security, and that natural gas is required to steady the grid.
  • According to recent reports, russian strikes are pounding the conventional energy infrastructure that Ukrainians depend upon to survive the winter, raising fears that some cities, among them the capital, Kyiv, could become uninhabitable.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

Russian strikes are pounding the conventional energy infrastructure that Ukrainians depend upon to survive the winter, raising fears that some cities, among them the capital, Kyiv, could become uninhabitable. With exactly this horror scenario in mind, Ukraine raced this spring and summer to expand decentralized energy systems—mostly small gas-fired power plants and renewable energy systems—to replace its bulky, big-target coal-fired plants as a way of better ensuring energy supply for critical infrastructure.

Government officials and most analysts in Ukraine concur that renewables and nuclear will underpin the country’s energy and national security, and that natural gas is required to steady the grid. But despite record rollouts of decentralized generation systems this year, the shift to a resilient energy grid is moving far more slowly than the winter and the war demand.

According to recent reports, russian strikes are pounding the conventional energy infrastructure that Ukrainians depend upon to survive the winter, raising fears that some cities, among them the capital, Kyiv, could become uninhabitable. With exactly this horror scenario in mind, Ukraine raced this spring and summer to expand decentralized energy systems—mostly small gas-fired power plants and renewable energy systems—to replace its bulky, big-target coal-fired plants as a way of better ensuring energy supply for critical infrastructure.

Government officials and most analysts in Ukraine concur that renewables and nuclear will underpin the country’s energy and national security, and that natural gas is required to steady the grid. But despite record rollouts of decentralized generation systems this year, the shift to a resilient energy grid is moving far more slowly than the winter and the war demand.

Under unusually dire wartime conditions, Ukraine expanded its total renewable generation capacity by roughly 16 percent by mid-2026 compared to early 2025. The country added 70 wind turbines in the first half of the year, mostly in the Mykolaiv and Odesa regions, and is presently bringing online a wind power plant close to the Black Sea, the largest wind farm ever built in a country at war.

Ukraine also added enough of solar generation to its supply this year to power roughly 600,000 to 800,000 European households, with European countries bankrolling rooftop solar-plus-battery systems for over 100 healthcare  facilities. Ukraine’s battery storage rollout in 2025 outpaced every EU member state save Germany and Italy while homeowner and business investment helped make Ukraine Europe’s fourth-largest battery storage market, a fivefold increase over 2024.

In a recent development, “Decentralized energy resources,” Maxim Timchenko—the CEO of DTEK, Ukraine’s largest utility—told the World Economic Forum earlier this year, “like wind, solar and energy storage. … are not only clean technologies, but they are also more resilient infrastructure. Smaller, distributed assets are harder to target, quicker to repair and more capable of stabilizing the grid during emergencies.”.

According to recent reports, while DTEK operates coal-fired power plants, too, Timchenko argued that renewable energy and battery storage will be the pillars of Ukraine’s long-term energy security and national defense—and the sooner that it builds them out, the better. And yet, DTEK commits more resources to restoring thermal plants and mining coal than to renewable or gas-fired systems.

According to recent reports, “Restoring the existing conventional heating supply is a much simpler and faster solution, especially in the current circumstances,” said Ukrainian energy expert Mykhailo Lukianyk. “A larger makeover of Ukraine’s energy sector requires more investment, planning, and time.”.

Nobody thinks a single energy source fits for a Ukraine at war. “It’s close to impossible,” said Andriy Martynyuk, director of Ecoclub, an energy NGO in Ukraine, “to find a single all-purpose solution that handles our harsh winters, delivers both heat and electricity, and can withstand jet-powered drones.”.

Although Kyiv’s grim plight captures the headlines, just about every urban center in Ukraine is facing a desperate winter. In the northwestern region of Rivne, emergency outages this month have darkened whole districts, although the region’s periodic stoppages have been less painful than the rolling blackouts elsewhere.

Sources indicate that the lights of Rivne’s City Center Hospital, for example, haven’t ebbed or flickered this fall: a testament to the work that renewables do in Rivne and in more than 300 other healthcare centers across the country. The hospital’s 214 panels cover two roofs and, paired with storage batteries in the cellars—courtesy largely of the German government—keep critical lifesaving operations humming during blackouts, even when Russian strikes hit transformer stations and upend the grid. None of Ukraine’s hospitals, however, boast renewable-powered systems that do more than back up operating rooms, intensive care, and elevators.

It has been revealed that in Rivne this year, the city bolted as much battery-supported solar power as it could onto roofs or mounted it in yards. When they’re full, the City Center Hospital’s batteries give it with enough energy to operate critical stations for four hours without grid power. When the batteries run out, more costly and less reliable diesel-fueled generators spring on, as they do in hospitals across the country. Another Rivne institution, the Regional Clinical Hospital, has been equipped with solar and battery installations since 2025 and survived last winter without going dark or cold once.

“The entire city is better prepared this winter,” said Artem Hanushchak, Rivne’s deputy mayor, who noted that last year, electricity was so tight that city hall urged owners of solar energy systems to clear the snow from their panels. “The system needed every bit of extra energy after Russian strikes,” he told Foreign Policy.

Rivne now also boasts an intelligent energy monitoring system that tracks energy use across 188 public buildings. Built by local and international IT specialists with $1 million in EU funding, it collects meter data to give city managers a real-time picture of electricity, heating, water, and gas use; supports the city’s emissions-reduction planning; and generates recommended energy upgrades.

In addition to security, renewables’ huge advantage, Hanushchak remarked, is their low cost, particularly with the price of gas remaining so high. Studies show that healthcare facilities with solar and batteries cut energy costs by as much as 70 percent —and the more panels and the bigger the battery, the more they save.

November is a particularly difficult month for Ukraine’s hospitals and solar energy alike. Solar panels produce only a fraction of their capacity during overcast Ukrainian days and, of course, produce nothing over the long nights. Hospitals require copious heat, which solar panels can’t easily supply at scale. Solar can heat buildings with heat pumps, which are ever more common across Ukraine, but not yet in the Rivne hospitals.

The other pillar of Ukraine’s energy security stratagem is small, modular, gas-fired cogeneration plants, which produce electricity and district heat simultaneously. Hanushchak argued that despite their vulnerability to attack—harder to hit than conventional thermal plants but larger targets than renewables—gas plants are key for Rivne and all of Ukraine. The Rivne region erected eight new cogeneration plants this year that burn natural gas to generate electricity while channeling excess heat into local district heating grids.

In a recent development, as impressive as Ukraine’s renewables rollout has been, it falls far short of its energy security ambitions. The Euromaidan Press wrote that Volodymyr Kudrytskyi, the former head of the grid operator Ukrenergo and presently head of a decentralized energy infrastructure firm, called the distributed generation program “effectively a failure” at the required scale. Rather than endlessly repairing 10 to 15 aging, easily targeted power plants, he has argued, Ukraine needs a balanced network of flexible gas, renewables, and storage—which is “dozens of times harder to scout and destroy.”.

Even though hospitals and health centers were prioritized, fewer than half of Ukraine’s healthcare facilities own panels and batteries, and not one of them is completely independent of the grid, even for a matter of hours. In June, the Razumkov Center pointed to a wide gap between Ukraine’s significant plans for 2026 and what is getting done. While international partners have donated 2.4 billion euros to the Ukraine Energy Support Fund since 2022 (including nearly 800 million euros in fresh contributions so far this year), the funding still falls short of the scale of destruction.

“A larger makeover of Ukraine’s energy sector requires more investment, planning, and time,” said Lukianyk, the energy expert. “Quite simply,” he added, “the demand for distributed solutions far outpaces our capacity to build or afford them.”.

Ukraine’s plans to outfit all hospitals, water utilities, and communication networks this year with distributed energy—the large part of a “new resilience architecture,” with an estimated cost of about $6.3 billion—fell short. The trouble began, as it did last year, when financing dried up. The Rivne hospitals’ green energy technology cost about $1 million per institution. The municipality chipped in, but never could have covered the cost—and cannot substantially upgrade it—without assistance from European donors. Ecoclub estimates that a $4.5 million investment in solar systems, batteries, and heat pumps would cover half of the Central City Hospital’s energy requirements.

On their own, Ukrainian developers struggle to raise international capital because war-risk insurance and guarantees remain limited. Moreover, many European firms are reluctant to finance or build projects in an active war zone, according to EUobserver. On the domestic market, companies face steep interest rates and punitive, short-term repayment schedules that render major wind and solar builds financially unviable. As the Razumkov Center noted, local banks remain deeply risk-averse, which effectively locks smaller players out of the market altogether.

The International Energy Agency (IEA) has commended Ukraine’s push to deploy solar, wind, and battery storage as a vital strategy for wartime energy resilience. But it, too, underscored in a new report that this year’s build-out was a fraction of what’s called for. Ukraine’s go-to strategies to keep the lights and heat on and the water running this winter, the IEA argued, are energy imports and local cogeneration.

In the end, the IEA concluded, “Air defence remains essential for maintaining the energy system.”.

Paul Hockenos is a Berlin-based journalist. His recent book is Berlin Calling: A Story of Anarchy, Music, the Wall, and the Birth of the New Berlin.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, tensions escalate in the Middle East as President Donald Trump signals his willingness to resume military strikes against Iran next year following recent drone attacks. Fox News chief foreign correspondent Trey Yingst reports live from Tel Aviv on the retaliatory claims, while retired Navy SEAL officer Mike Sarraille discusses the conflict during 'The Faulkner Focus.'.

FIRST ON FOX: The Treasury Department on Monday imposed sweeping newly introduced sanctions against more than two dozen Iranian exchange houses, overseas front companies and financial operatives accused of moving billions of dollars through a global "shadow banking" network to keep Iran connected to international trade.

According to recent reports, the action, carried out by the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), targeted "financial plumbing" spanning Iran, Dubai, Hong Kong and Turkey that officials say enables Tehran to bypass U. S. restrictions, sell oil and petrochemicals, and settle transactions in Russian rubles and Chinese yuan.

According to recent reports, "Iran’s economy is underwater, and its leaders are panicking," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent wrote in a statement Monday before the news release. "Iran’s shadow banking system is the last financial lifeline of a bankrupt regime. Treasury will continue dismantling these illicit networks until we have buried the head of the snake.".

TRUMP’S IRAN CRACKDOWN ‘SUFFOCATING’ REGIME AS OIL WELLS COULD SHUT WITHIN DAYS, BESSENT INDICATES.

Monday’s designations mark the latest escalation under Operation Economic Outcast, a maximum financial pressure campaign Bessent launched on Aug. 24, to cut off the regime's remaining revenue streams and heighten secondary sanctions risks for foreign banks and brokers that continue doing business with Tehran.

TRUMP'S FIRST IRAN WAR ESCALATION POST-MIDTERM LOSSES SEEKS TO CHOKE OFF TEHRAN’S TRADE.

Recent findings suggest that according to the Treasury Department, Iran's "shadow banking" apparatus is overseen by the Central Bank of Iran and relies on domestic currency exchange houses paired with bank-affiliated "rahbar companies" that manage sanctions-evasion networks through thousands of foreign shell firms. As declining oil revenues and existing sanctions squeeze the Iranian economy, Treasury noted shadow banking facilitators have increasingly failed to repatriate export earnings while enriching themselves with state funds.

The Treasury also revealed Monday that its Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) "identified approximately $14.7 billion of financial activity from January 2025 to August 2026 potentially linked to Iranian shadow banking.".

MILLIONS OF BARRELS OF IRANIAN OIL SIT BEYOND TRUMP BLOCKADE AS HE VOWS ‘ZERO LEAKAGE’.

Among the highest-profile targets in Monday’s package is the Iran-based Iran Center for Exchange of Currency and Gold, which matches Iranian exporters holding foreign currency with importers seeking to buy goods abroad across tens of billions of dollars in annual trade. Treasury noted that the Central Bank of Iran also uses bonds issued by the exchange center to facilitate cross-border trade in Russian rubles and Chinese yuan without relying on the U.S. dollar.

BESSENT WARNS IRAN'S OUTSIDE BACKERS TO 'STAY AWAY' AS TRUMP SEEKS TO 'ASPHYXIATE' TEHRAN'S ECONOMY.

Sources indicate that the OFAC package sanctions Rahbar Bazargani Nesim Baharan Qeshm Manufacturer — the rahbar affiliate for Iran’s Bank Sarmayeh — along with three of its senior officials, Sayyed Mohammad Jalali, Valiollah Hemmati and Ali Kalhor, for facilitating transactions on behalf of major Iranian oil companies. Two Iran-based currency dealers, Mina Fashki and Partners Exchange Company and Mellat Exchange Company, were blacklisted alongside five of their owners and officials.

US TARGETS CHINESE REFINERY IN SWEEPING IRAN OIL CRACKDOWN, SANCTIONS ‘SHADOW FLEET’ TANKERS.

Industry observers note that to choke off Tehran's overseas payment channels, Treasury targeted 10 exchange house front companies across the United Arab Emirates, Turkey and Hong Kong accused of moving billions of dollars for Iranian clients. Those include Dubai-based Recaz Star General Trading LLC, which sent and received hundreds of payments totaling more than $170 million tied to Sadaf Exchange, and OGA Global General Trading L. L. C, which oversaw millions of dollars in payments for the state-owned National Iranian Tanker Tech giant.

Other newly sanctioned front companies include Hong Kong-based Grandez Trading Limited, Turkey-based Bogazici Gumrukleme Ithalat Ihracat Turizm Petrol Urunleri Sanayi Ve Ticaret Limited Sirketi and several Dubai-based trading firms — including Gespl International General Trading LLC, which Treasury alleged was used by the National Iranian Oil Company to launder oil and petrochemical proceeds, and Robust Trading LLC for processing payments for the sanctioned National Iranian Copper Industries Company.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, JOSHUA A. SCHWARTZ is Assistant Professor of International Relations and Emerging Technology at the Carnegie Mellon Institute for Strategy & Technology.

How Fighting Weakens Washington’s Reputation—and Backing Down May Strengthen It.

In mid-February, after the United States failed to get Iran to renounce its nuclear ambitions, U.S. President Donald Trump issued an ultimatum. The Iranian leadership had to make “a meaningful deal” with Washington. “Otherwise,” he said, “bad things happen.” Barely eight days later, the United States and Israel began the war against Iran that continues today.

It has been revealed that that war has been criticized on many grounds, but analysts have often overlooked the basic assumption about U.S. credibility that it has tested. There is a long-held understanding that the United States’ willingness to use force to stand up for its interests is essential to deterring future adversaries—and convincing them to give in to the kind of sweeping demands the Trump administration made of Tehran. As Elbridge Colby, U.S. undersecretary of defense for policy, remarked in the early stages of the conflict, “I think both our friends and potential foes are seeing the prowess of the joint force and that also contributes to deterrence.”.

Going back to the early years of the Cold War, the concept of credibility—a state’s perceived capabilities and its willingness to use them even at high cost—has played a central role in the decisions that led to and sustained many of the United States’ largest military campaigns. The need to bolster U.S. credibility was a key force driving Washington’s strategy in Korea and Vietnam in the mid-twentieth century, and it played an vital role in Iraq and Afghanistan during the so-called war on terror. American strategists today continue to assess foreign policy decisions based on how they might strengthen or weaken the country’s reputation.

In a recent development, but as the results of the Iran campaign have shown, a decision to use force does not always strengthen deterrence. After nearly ten months of war, and the expenditure of billions of dollars of munitions, the United States appears little closer to achieving its objectives of definitively ending Iran’s nuclear threat and ability to project power across the region, let alone securing regime change in Tehran. Meanwhile, the war has badly depleted U.S. military resources that could be used elsewhere and has further eroded the American public’s willingness to support military interventions. Rather than sending a strong signal of U.S. resolve, the Iran war risks conveying the opposite message. Vice President JD Vance argued that the reason the Republicans lost the midterm elections was the Iran war, and government officials in Tehran have gloated that “Americans noted no to war.”.

In fact, the conventional wisdom that standing firm in a military conflict enhances a state’s credibility misses something vital. As the U.S. wars in Vietnam and Iraq showed, a prolonged military campaign may leave the country more cautious about using force, and less willing to bear the costs, in the years that follow. Adversaries notice this. Given that prior efforts by the Trump administration to compromise with Tehran were criticized as “appeasement” by figures like former U.S. Vice President Mike Pence, Trump may be tempted to continue or even expand the Iran campaign. But by taxing U.S. capabilities and deepening war-weariness among the American public, escalation in Iran could instead lead Beijing and Moscow to question Washington’s appetite for future interventions.

According to recent reports, policymakers should be far more skeptical about using military force for the sake of demonstrating U.S. resolve, and they should be less averse to backing down. The Cold War competition with the Soviet Union convinced the United States to intervene in costly proxy wars that consumed enormous human and military resources for questionable gain, and now the strategic competition with China and Russia may do the same. These kinds of conflicts are precisely the ones that are likely to harm, rather than help, U.S. credibility. Instead of obsessing about its reputation for resolve, which it cannot control, Washington must refocus its attention on maintaining the military strength and capabilities it needs to deter its major adversaries. Sometimes the best way to preserve both the capability and the willingness to act in the future is to walk away from conflict in the present.

For decades, policymakers and scholars have treated a country’s credibility as the dark matter of international politics—a hard-to-measure attribute that is nonetheless enormously important for maintaining deterrence. In the 1960s, nuclear deterrence theorist and Nobel Prize winner Thomas Schelling went so far as to say that acquiring a reputation for resolve is “one of the few things worth fighting over.” In keeping with this, it has long been assumed that whereas standing firm communicates to adversaries and allies alike that a country is willing to run risks and bear costs to uphold its interests, backing down or seeking to compromise conveys the opposite. As a result, many U.S. leaders and strategists have drawn on the logic of credibility to justify the most hawkish policies toward adversaries: making maximalist demands, using force, and remaining in wars long past the point where their costs exceeded their benefits.

Industry observers note that vietnam was a case in point. When debating whether to send the first group of U.S. troops to Vietnam in 1965, U.S. Secretary of State Dean Rusk told President Lyndon Johnson, “If the Communist world finds out we will not pursue our commitments to the end, I don’t know where they will stay their hand.” Later, as the United States became bogged down in the war, Assistant Secretary of Defense John McNaughton went further, arguing in a formerly top-secret memo that the primary reason for continuing the Vietnam War was to maintain America’s “reputation as a guarantor” and “avoid a humiliating U.S. defeat.” According to this logic, 58,000 U.S. soldiers and likely over a million Vietnamese people were killed not because the outcome of the war was itself crucial to U.S. interests, but because Washington worried how others—especially the Soviets—would perceive it if it withdrew.

Since the Cold War, the same justifications have been used to push the country into, and to sustain, many other conflicts. This was especially true during the so-called Forever Wars the United States was drawn into after the 9/11 attacks. On the night of 9/11, U.S. Secretary of Defense Donald Rumsfeld said, “We need to bomb something else [other than the relatively weak Taliban] to prove that we’re, you know, big and strong and not going to be pushed around by these kinds of attacks.” The logic of credibility not only played a role in Washington launching the Iraq war in 2003 but also locked it into the conflict, even as the costs rose and the raison d’être for the war—weapons of mass destruction—turned out to be false. As President George W. Bush said in 2006, “If we were to leave before the mission is complete, it would hurt U.S. credibility.”.

Conversely, strategists have been quick to criticize U.S. leaders who backed down. During the Syrian civil war, many were concerned about the reputational damage to the United States when President Barack Obama declined to respond to the Syrian government’s use of sarin gas to attack a rebel-held suburb of Damascus, thereby violating a red line that Obama had previously declared. In 2021, many foreign policy hawks reprimanded President Joe Biden for withdrawing from Afghanistan and for waiving some U.S. sanctions on Russia’s Nord Stream 2 pipeline project. At the time, Michael McCaul, the top Republican on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, noted, “U.S. credibility from Kyiv to Taipei cannot withstand another blow of this nature.” More recently, Trump himself has been accused of backing down against China on tariffs, which some have decried as another example of “Trump always chickens out,” or “TACO.” In each of these cases, critics argued that Washington’s failure to act has compromised the perception that the United States is willing to run risks and bear costs to achieve its objectives.

It has been revealed that despite the persistent assumption that U.S. credibility requires using force and refusing to back down, that thinking has been repeatedly challenged over the past decade. For one thing, experience has shown that a country’s past behavior may be a poor indicator of its present-day resolve. In April, for example, The New York Times reported that Trump believed that Iran was unlikely to attempt to close the Strait of Hormuz based on its past actions—such as its failure to mount a robust response to the U.S. and Israeli bombing of its nuclear facilities in the 12-day war in 2025. In reality, however, Iran has been far less restrained than expected in the current conflict and moved swiftly not only to close the strait but also to attack U.S. allies and U.S. military bases across the region. In other words, Tehran’s failure to stand firm in 2025 had little bearing on its resolve in the present war.

According to recent reports, in any case, it is far from clear that a country’s reputation for resolve is something that it can control by its actions alone. As Keren Yarhi-Milo has explained in Foreign Affairs, “credibility is in the eye of the beholder.” Even if a state acts decisively to signal strength, an adversary may not interpret that action as reason to reconsider its behavior. For example, despite Washington’s intention to communicate high resolve by bearing tremendous costs in the Vietnam War, the North Vietnamese Communist Party Central Committee concluded in 1965 that “the domestic situation in the United States, however, will not allow them to fully utilize their economic and military power in their war of aggression.” In other words, Hanoi ignored the intended signal from Washington and refused to back down.

Recent findings suggest that other pitfalls are associated with demonstrating resolve by standing firm and fighting. At the extreme, a state that leans too much on military strength can gain a reputation for aggression in ways that undermine long-term deterrence. Napoleonic France and Nazi Germany both had strong reputations for resolve, but their offensive actions ultimately provoked other countries rather than deterring them. There is certainly a risk that U.S. actions under the second Trump administration—such as decapitating the Iranian government and threatening to annex Canada, Gaza, and Greenland—could similarly backfire. For example, there is growing evidence that U.S. allies and partners in Europe, the Middle East, and Asia are rethinking their reliance on the United States and are seeking other sources of security. Far from conceding to Trump’s demands, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has described a “rupture” in relations between Washington and Ottawa and advocated for middle powers to band together to protect their sovereignty.

Even if using force bolsters a country’s reputation for resolve, it may harm the country’s broader credibility. For instance, Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine and its willingness to absorb hundreds of thousands of casualties since then has sent a strong signal about its resolve. Yet its dramatic underperformance on the battlefield against a far smaller and less well-equipped army has likely diminished the international perception of its military effectiveness. The war in Iran could similarly tarnish the United States’ military reputation. Since February, Washington has depleted at least half of its precision-strike missiles and advanced air defense interceptor missiles. It will likely take years to replenish these stockpiles given slow manufacturing times for so-called exquisite platforms. In the meantime, the United States has fewer advanced systems to draw on if China makes a move against Taiwan or if Russia attacks Poland or Estonia. For both Russia’s and the United States’ military campaigns, then, the net effect has been to reduce rather than enhance the countries’ reputation for military capability in the eyes of their respective adversaries.

Quite apart from the negative consequences that often come with decisions to use force, there is an even more fundamental problem with conventional thinking about credibility. In practice, backing down can actually be more helpful to a country’s reputation for resolve than fighting. This becomes especially clear in looking at the long-term effects of engaging in military interventions. Although the United States was victorious in World War I, the conflict produced a lingering war-weariness among the U.S. public and key policymakers. In the years after the Armistice, Americans expressed strong support for the idea that the United States should stay out of any future European war, a sentiment that was ultimately codified in the Neutrality Acts of the 1930s. Only after Japan attacked Pearl Harbor in December 1941, more than two years after war began in Europe, did the United States enter World War II. Fighting in World War I sent a signal of strong resolve to adversaries, but Americans’ war-weariness and resurgent isolationism in the years that followed conveyed that the United States would be less resolved to fight.

According to recent reports, this dynamic has been even more apparent in the aftermath of major U.S. wars since then. Following the Vietnam War, President Jimmy Carter declared that “young Americans should never again be sent to die in battle unless our own nation is endangered.” Consider how this kind of thinking affected adversaries’ view of the United States: In deciding to invade Kuwait in 1990, Iraqi dictator Saddam Hussein assumed that the United States was intensely casualty averse and might not intervene or would back down quickly. General Wafiq al-Samarrai, Iraq’s head of military intelligence during the Gulf War, remarked in a 1996 interview that Saddam “thought that America’s involvement in Vietnam had badly damaged its willingness to use military power.” Although the Vietnam War was primarily fought to buttress the United States’ reputation for resolve, it had the opposite effect in practice.

It has been revealed that and again, during and after the U.S. war in Iraq, Americans became skeptical of costly military interventions. As a result, recent administrations have been especially hesitant to commit ground troops in combat operations. Iran is undoubtedly aware of this so-called Iraq syndrome, which may embolden Tehran to act more aggressively without having to fear a large-scale American ground operation.

There is also experimental evidence that backing down may strengthen a country’s long-term reputation for resolve. In a survey I conducted in 2021 with 100 British parliamentarians, respondents were randomly divided into two groups. The first group read about a situation in which a hypothetical country backed down from a prior conflict. The second group read about a hypothetical country that stood firm in a prior conflict but displayed the same signs of war-weariness or “syndromes” that emerged in the United States after the Vietnam and Iraq wars. Both groups were then asked to estimate the likelihood that the country in question would stand firm or back down in a current dispute with the United Kingdom. On average, parliamentarians believed that the country that backed down in the prior dispute would have greater resolve in the current dispute. In other words, if fighting leads to war-weariness, then backing down can actually be better for a state’s future credibility.

In a recent development, as the U.S. campaign in Iran has demonstrated, choosing to fight to maintain a reputation for resolve is an incredibly risky gamble and may backfire. To avoid repeating the same mistake, U.S. policymakers and strategists need to rethink the relationship between credibility and fighting. First, the United States should avoid fighting altogether when the primary objective is shoring up reputation rather than defending a core national issue. If a conflict directly involves key security and economic interests, as did the U.S. Revolutionary War and World War II, then fighting can be a logical choice, assuming the United States has sufficient military capabilities to win the war at reasonable cost. But if the primary argument for the war relates to future credibility, as in Vietnam, then policymakers should be wary.

Second, if Washington determines that an adversary must be confronted with military force, then it must focus on limited, achievable objectives. Wars that drag on because they have much larger aims, or are prolonged simply for reputational reasons, may erode the country’s credibility by draining munitions and making Americans more reluctant to fight in the future. The two U.S. interventions against Saddam Hussein’s Iraq illustrate this point well. In the limited 1991 Gulf War, the United States swiftly expelled Iraqi forces from Kuwait at low cost and before war-weariness could set in among the U.S. public. But the U.S.-led invasion of Iraq in 2003, in which Washington pursued the far more expansive goal of regime change, continued for years at high cost and made many U.S. policymakers and ordinary citizens alike less supportive of using force in the future.

Finally, policymakers should focus less on the U.S. reputation for resolve, which they cannot control, and more on the country’s military capabilities, which they can. To deter Beijing and Moscow, Washington needs to convince both adversaries that it has the ability to prosecute a modern great-power war. The problem is that, although the United States continues to have the most advanced military capabilities and weapons systems in the world, they are limited in quantity, extremely expensive, and take a long time to replace. In the course of just a few months of fighting against Iran, the United States depleted huge percentages of its advanced and expensive stockpiles of offensive and defensive missiles.

According to recent reports, this alarming shortfall raises upcoming questions about whether the United States could sustain a longer war of attrition of the type Russia and Ukraine are fighting. Washington urgently needs to replenish its stockpiles and rethink its dependence on a small number of exquisite systems. It also needs to avoid costly conflicts that distract it from the principal threats it faces from China and Russia. Rather than making U.S. credibility stronger in the eyes of the world, continuing the war in Iran could well undermine it, just as fighting in Vietnam and Iraq did.

Democrats Want to Make Life More Affordable. They Could Begin With Permitting Reform.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

The Democratic wave that shook the U.S. political landscape this month delivered a striking rebuke to President Donald Trump and put affordability squarely at the top of the political agenda. A bill that passed the Senate last week to reform the nation’s permitting laws offers Democrats—who voted two-to-one against the bill in the Senate—an early test of whether they can make daily life more affordable for Americans, even before taking control in January. Permitting reform may seem like a narrow or technical topic, but this is the most important piece of energy legislation in years. By speeding up environmental reviews, limiting litigation delays, and easing transmission siting, it would expand clean energy, lower energy prices, strengthen our energy system, and make future climate action more effective.

The bill, known as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, would make it easier to build transmission lines and other energy infrastructure, including both clean energy and oil and gas projects. That breadth has delighted advocates of abundance, the movement that argues that shortcomings in public infrastructure stem from regulatory bottlenecks, and enraged many environmentalists. Some supporters have been too quick to dismiss legitimate concerns, while some climate activists have drowned out substantive but highly technical legal objections with reflexive anti-fossil fuel rhetoric. As the bill heads to a House vote, a careful assessment of its provisions should lead members to support it while pursuing opportunities where possible to address credible objections in the final stages of the legislative process.

The Democratic wave that shook the U.S. political landscape this month delivered a striking rebuke to President Donald Trump and put affordability squarely at the top of the political agenda. A bill that passed the Senate last week to reform the nation’s permitting laws offers Democrats—who voted two-to-one against the bill in the Senate—an early test of whether they can make daily life more affordable for Americans, even before taking control in January. Permitting reform may seem like a narrow or technical topic, but this is the most important piece of energy legislation in years. By speeding up environmental reviews, limiting litigation delays, and easing transmission siting, it would expand clean energy, lower energy prices, strengthen our energy system, and make future climate action more effective.

The bill, known as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, would make it easier to build transmission lines and other energy infrastructure, including both clean energy and oil and gas projects. That breadth has delighted advocates of abundance, the movement that argues that shortcomings in public infrastructure stem from regulatory bottlenecks, and enraged many environmentalists. Some supporters have been too quick to dismiss legitimate concerns, while some climate activists have drowned out substantive but highly technical legal objections with reflexive anti-fossil fuel rhetoric. As the bill heads to a House vote, a careful assessment of its provisions should lead members to support it while pursuing opportunities where possible to address credible objections in the final stages of the legislative process.

Objections to the permitting reform bill fall into several broad categories. First, some Democrats and environmental groups argue that the blue election wave gives them leverage to secure a better deal next year, yet that misreads both the politics and the policy. A larger Democratic majority does not necessarily mean a majority for blocking fossil fuel infrastructure. The incoming caucus includes members who support oil and gas development alongside clean energy—in states such as Texas, Mississippi, Kansas, South Carolina, and Alaska. Nor does 56 Senate seats eliminate the need for Republican votes to overcome a filibuster. And Trump will still be president, with the power to veto the bill.

Second, some environmental groups oppose the bill because it weakens tools of environmental review and permitting often used to block fossil fuel projects such as oil and gas pipelines. Yet ample evidence demonstrates that trying to “keep it in the ground”—stymying fossil fuel supply by blocking infrastructure—does little to reduce global oil and gas use, which ultimately is what matters for greenhouse gas emissions, and can trigger backlash to climate action if energy security and affordability are perceived to suffer as a result.

In a global market, supply restrictions in one location merely lead to increases elsewhere unless demand falls. Higher prices can curb demand, but this year’s energy crisis offers further evidence that political and economic pressures push elected leaders to use every available tool to bring prices back down. The Iran war led to the closure of much of the Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly 20 percent of the world’s oil flowed, yet oil demand this year will drop only 2.5 percent, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA).

While it is possible—and necessary—to reduce the need for oil and gas over the long term, today fossil fuels still supply roughly four-fifths of the world’s energy, a figure that has barely changed in decades. While reducing that dependence is urgently needed to address the rapidly escalating threats of climate change, the hard reality is that keeping energy affordable and reliable during a multidecade transition still requires investment in oil and gas. According to the IEA, around $490 billion a year would still be needed by 2035 even in a scenario where countries meet their climate pledges—which the collapse of United Nations climate talks in Turkey made plainly clear is far from being true today.

It has been revealed that moreover, the same strategies used against high-profile pipelines such as Keystone XL and Mountain Valley have often proved effective at obstructing clean energy projects as well. As the New York Times editorial board argued this month in endorsing permitting reform, essential laws protecting the environment, communities, and Indigenous peoples “have become so complex and restrictive that the country cannot build the future it needs.”.

To be sure, the BAAJA is not a substitute for climate policy, nor are its emissions benefits assured. Analysis by Rhodium Group, a consultancy, projects that the bill could reduce U.S. power-sector emissions in 2040 by as much as 18 percent compared with current policy, or by as little as 1 percent, depending on energy prices and technology costs. At the same time, climate policy cannot be effective without a bill such as the BAAJA that allows for the rapid buildout of the generation, transmission, storage, and transit infrastructure required for cleaner energy solutions.

A third area of concern involves weakened tribal consultation under the National Historic Preservation Act. Faster permitting should not undermine tribes’ ability to meaningfully influence decisions that affect sacred sites and other places central to their history and traditions. A set of revisions to the bill would have expanded the projects subject to tribal consultation and authorized additional money to support tribal and state historic-preservation work, yet Democratic Senator Jeff Merkley prevented those amendments from being considered, which may make it harder for some House Democrats to support the bill.

Expanding the U.S. grid is vital to staying globally competitive.

According to recent reports, ones and Tooze on permitting reform and what that means for U.S. energy production.

It has been revealed that finally, some opponents worry that specific provisions could protect improperly approved projects, require the government to pay companies large sums in damages, and constrain future administrations’ ability to problem or enforce environmental protections. Because these objections involve detailed, often technical, legal objections to the bill’s drafting, they have failed to garner the same attention as absolutist rhetoric about fossil fuels or misleading claims about data center buildout, which is unfortunate because many of these legal concerns have merit, even if they do not ultimately justify opposing the bill.

Recent findings suggest that at the heart of critics’ concerns is a mistrust of how a conservative judiciary hostile to environmental regulation will interpret the bill’s ambiguities. Key areas of concern include new limits on National Environmental Policy Act lawsuits and potential unintended consequences of provisions to limit an administration’s ability to revoke existing permits. Those so-called permit certainty provisions, which the New Yorker’s Elizabeth Kolbert called the most “dangerous” in the bill, were designed to prevent just the sort of harm the Trump administration has done to offshore wind.

Yet subsequent revisions to the bill, known as the “manager’s amendment,” made meaningful improvements to address those concerns. Kolbert writes that the bill could “tie the hands of any future Administration that wants to responsibly promote green energy over fossil fuels,” yet the revisions specifically added an exception to address this concern for agency actions taken under applicable law or regulation and a clause intended to preserve existing legal authorities. They responded to concerns that restrictions on government interference with a permitted project’s operation at “full capacity” could be used to block new environmental rules—for example, emissions standards under the Clean Air Act that would induce a coal plant to curb its output. The amendment also extends from five to 10 years the permitting-data lookback used to assess claims of disparate treatment. That longer time period addressed concerns that Trump’s preferential treatment of fossil fuels and obstruction of renewables would become the benchmark against which a future administration’s permitting decisions are judged.

It has been revealed that the changes also require a showing of bad faith for the additional damages available under the bill, addressing concerns that an agency could face enormous payouts for an action a court finds unlawful. And the amendment expressly allows the government to offer lawful explanations for differences in permitting outcomes and extends the requirement that applicants seeking relief demonstrate technical and financial capacity to all of their pending projects.

But the changes do not eliminate every risk. For example, an expansive interpretation of what counts as a “permit” or “authorization” could, critics fear, extend protections beyond formal agency approvals to informal assurances from the Trump administration. Critics also worry that because nearly every agency action invokes some legal authority, a broad reading of the exception for actions “taken pursuant to any applicable law or regulation” could render the permit protections meaningless. To avoid that result, judges could read the exception narrowly, limiting future administrations’ ability to curb pollution.

Recent findings suggest that another round of revisions—the one blocked by Merkley—would have made modest improvements, such as to the concern about private assurances counting as authorizations. The legal risks identified about how hostile judges could interpret ambiguity merit attention and should be remedied to the extent possible as the current bill moves through Congress. Although the bill is unlikely to be amended in the House, one of its architects in the Senate has suggested the House might attach amendments to other pieces of must-pass legislation.

Even without those revisions, however, the bill’s benefits outweigh the risks. The current permitting system simply makes it too difficult and costly to expand the grid, build a stronger energy system, connect cleaner generation, and lower energy costs.

Later this week, Americans will gather for Thanksgiving, with energy costs weighing on the price of traveling to see family, heating homes, and cooking the holiday meal. The annual national observance of Thanksgiving started with President Abraham Lincoln’s proclamation in 1863—the same year construction began on the transcontinental railroad. Six years later, the two lines met in Utah, connecting nearly 1,800 miles of track. By contrast, California today aims to begin high-speed rail service between Merced and Bakersfield—a distance of less than 200 miles—in 2033, a quarter-century after voters approved the project. When members of Congress return from their Thanksgiving celebrations, their first order of business should be to make it easier to build again in this country—starting with the infrastructure needed for a cleaner, more affordable, and more reliable energy system.
